ai-harness

ai-harness

A terminal agent harness for models served through OpenRouter. The prompt is pinned to the bottom; the conversation scrolls above it. The distinguishing idea is that the model may not reply with free text — every reply must be exactly one of six XML elements, validated by a strict parser.

6,446 lines of code across 16 files, plus 6,186 lines of tests. Every non-test line is annotated in the tabs on the left, in reading order rather than alphabetical order. This page is the map you need before opening any of them.

The contract

Your prompt goes out wrapped:

<ai-harness-query>count the rust files in src</ai-harness-query>

The model must reply with exactly one of these, and nothing else — no prose, no markdown fence, no second element:

ElementMeaningApproval
<ai-harness-read>Read one fileNone — runs immediately
<ai-harness-fetch>Read one web pageNone — runs immediately
<ai-harness-shell>Run a shell commandModal
<ai-harness-write>Write a whole fileModal, with a preview
<ai-harness-edit>Replace one exact spanModal, with a diff
<ai-harness-response>Final answer — ends the turnn/a

Anything else is rejected rather than guessed at, and the model gets a targeted correction and retries — up to three times, after which the whole failed exchange is rolled back out of context. See protocol.rs.

The agentic loop, end to end

The loop is not a loop construct anywhere. It is this convention: a method on App returns Option<Vec<Message>>, and main.rs spawns a request whenever it gets Some. Five methods do that — push_command_result, push_write_result, perform_read, push_fetch_result, and deny — plus retry_after on a malformed reply.

<ai-harness-fetch> is the one action that does not fit that convention, and it is worth knowing why. It is auto-approved like a read, so nothing is pending and the turn has not ended — but it is network I/O, so App cannot just do it and hand back the messages. It parks the URL in pending_fetch, and the event loop collects it with take_pending_fetch. So a None from push_response now means "ask me what happened" rather than "the loop pauses here". The alternative was letting App spawn tasks, which would put tokio in the one file that has no I/O in it.

Who calls whom

Three files depend on nothing in the crate and are worth reading first if you want an easy start: wrap.rs (word wrapping), command.rs (no imports at all), and ledger.rs. They are pure functions with obvious contracts.

Two files are the hubs. app.rs holds all state and every transition; main.rs owns the terminal and the tokio tasks. Nothing else does I/O except the leaves that exist for it — exec, files, fetch, session, openrouter, tui.

Five mechanisms that span files

These are the things you cannot see by reading any single file, and they explain most of the code that would otherwise look over-careful.

1. Generation tagging — why cancel is safe

Every spawned task carries a counter. Cancelling bumps it, so updates the abandoned task already queued are recognised as stale and dropped rather than corrupting the next turn.

Cancellation is cooperative: the task also selects on a one-shot channel, and dropping the sender is enough to fire it — so replacing the in-flight handle cancels the old task automatically.

main.rs Tagged, InFlight · app.rs generation, next_generation, cancel

2. Retry and rollback — surviving a bad reply

A malformed reply gets a targeted correction quoting exactly what broke, and the model tries again. After --max-retries attempts the harness gives up and truncates history back to retry_anchor, rolling the whole failed exchange out of context.

The reasoning: leaving the model's own malformed output in context makes repeating it more likely. The transcript still shows what happened — it is hidden from the model, not from you.

app.rs retry_after, retry_anchor · protocol.rs encode_correction, ProtocolError

3. Entry vs Message — two records that diverge

history: Vec<Message> is what the model sees — protocol-wrapped, and sometimes rolled back. transcript: Vec<Entry> is what you see — including notices, errors, and raw frames that were never sent anywhere.

Watch them split in send_prompt: the transcript gets what you typed, history gets it wrapped in <ai-harness-query>. Both are saved, because you need one to keep talking and the other to restore your screen.

app.rs Entry, send_prompt · openrouter.rs Message · session.rs Session

4. Edit pre-flight — approve only what will apply

An edit is resolved against the file before the modal. plan_edit requires the old text to appear exactly once; zero or many matches is rejected and handed straight back to the model to fix, so you never see a modal for an edit that cannot apply.

The prepared rewrite rides in Pending.edit_plan, and approve converts it into a plain Write. The file is not re-read after approval — the bytes that land are exactly the ones the diff showed.

files.rs plan_edit, EditPlan · app.rs push_response, approve · ui.rs diff_lines

5. One denylist, two enforcement paths

Shell commands are confined by the macOS kernel via Seatbelt. Auto-approved reads are confined in-process by files::resolve. Those are completely different mechanisms — so both are driven from the same two constants in sandbox.rs, and cannot drift apart.

Reads are held to the stricter policy: shell may read anywhere outside the denylist, a read element may only touch the working-directory subtree. It has to be, since it ships file contents to OpenRouter without asking you.

sandbox.rs SECRET_HOME_SUBPATHS, SECRET_ROOT_FILES, denies_read, profile · files.rs resolve

Bonus: wrap it yourself, always

Both the editor and the transcript wrap text before handing it to ratatui, never letting Paragraph do it. That makes one Line exactly one screen row, so lines.len() is the true rendered height.

Everything downstream depends on that being exact: scroll clamping, stick-to-bottom, and putting the terminal cursor in the right cell.

wrap.rs · input.rs layout, locate · ui.rs draw_transcript

Where to start reading

Pick by what you are about to change.

If you want to…Read, in this order
Understand it at allThis page, then protocol.rs (the contract), then app.rs push_response (the decision), then main.rs handle_update (the loop)
Add a protocol elementprotocol.rs tag constants → Action → parse_reply → system_prompt, then app.rs push_response, then ui.rs render_entry
Add a slash commandcommand.rs Command + COMMANDS, then app.rs run_command. Two places, and the menu and /help update themselves
Change the displayui.rs — start at draw for layout or render_entry for content
Touch sandboxingsandbox.rs in full, then files.rs resolve, then exec.rs write_file. Note the shared-denylist contract before changing either side
Add a key bindingmain.rs handle_key — mind the guard order and the _ if app.is_busy() wall

main.rs

535 lines of code

The event loop. Owns the terminal, translates keys and background results into calls on App, and spawns the tokio tasks that do the slow work.

uses app, config, exec, openrouter, protocol, sandbox, tui, ui

used by nothing — it is the crate root

This is the only file that is allowed to be impure in the interesting sense: it talks to the terminal, spawns tasks, and owns the channel everything reports back on. Every other module is either pure state (app, input) or a self-contained capability (exec, openrouter).

The shape is a single loop that does three things forever: draw the frame, select! on whichever of three sources fires first (a terminal event, a background result, or a timer tick), then maybe auto-save. Everything else in the file is a handler called from that loop.

The one idea worth internalising before reading: generations. Every background task is tagged with a counter. Cancelling bumps the counter, so any update the abandoned task had already queued is recognised as stale and thrown away instead of corrupting the next turn.

const TICK

L35–L36

80 ms. This does double duty: it is the spinner's animation rate, and it is the ceiling on how long the UI can go without redrawing. Because the loop redraws at the top of every iteration, a tick that fires with nothing else pending still produces a frame.

35/// Spinner animation rate; also bounds how long we go without redrawing.
36const TICK: Duration = Duration::from_millis(80);

enum Update — what background work reports back

L37–L51

The five things a spawned task can tell the UI. Note that two of them (Delta, ReplyEnd) come from the same streaming request: deltas arrive many times, ReplyEnd exactly once at the end.

ReplyEnd, Command, and Write all carry a Result<_, String> rather than a real error type. The error has already been formatted with {e:#} (the anyhow "with all causes" form) inside the task, because the error may not be Send-friendly to carry across the channel and the UI only ever wants to print it.

Fetch joins them, and note the asymmetry: the others are Result<_, String>, this one is a bare FetchOutcome. A refused URL or an HTTP error is not a failure to do the work — it is the work's result, and the model should see it. There is nothing left for an Err to mean.

37 
38/// Something happened in the background and the UI needs to react.
39enum Update {
40 /// A chunk of streamed reply text.
41 Delta(String),
42 /// The model reply finished, or the error that replaced it.
43 ReplyEnd(Result<Completion, String>),
44 /// A sandboxed command finished, or failed to start.
45 Command(Result<CommandOutput, String>),
46 /// A sandboxed file write finished, or failed to start.
47 Write(Result<WriteOutcome, String>),
48 /// A URL fetch finished. Refusals and HTTP errors arrive as a `FetchOutcome`
49 /// carrying the reason, so `Err` here means the request never started.
50 Fetch(Box<FetchOutcome>),
51}

struct Tagged — the staleness guard

L52–L58

Every message on the channel carries the generation of the task that produced it. handle_update compares it against app.generation() and drops anything that does not match.

Why this exists: cancelling a task cannot un-send the messages it already put on the channel. Without the tag, pressing Esc mid-stream and immediately typing a new prompt would let the dead request's tokens leak into the new turn.
52 
53/// An [`Update`] tagged with the generation of the task that produced it, so a
54/// cancelled task's still-queued updates can be recognised as stale and dropped.
55struct Tagged {
56 generation: u64,
57 update: Update,
58}

struct InFlight — the cancel handle

L59–L64

A one-shot sender. The spawned task holds the matching receiver and select!s on it. Sending or dropping the sender resolves the receiver, so simply replacing inflight with a new handle cancels the old task — you cannot forget to cancel.

Only one task is ever in flight at a time, which is why this is a plain Option rather than a map.

59 
60/// A handle to the current in-flight task. Dropping or sending on `cancel`
61/// resolves the task's cancel future, stopping its work cleanly.
62struct InFlight {
63 cancel: oneshot::Sender<()>,
64}

struct Ctx — what the handlers need to start work

L65–L76

Bundled so the handler signatures stay short. client and sandbox are both cheap to clone() into a task (the client wraps a reqwest::Client, which is an Arc internally; the sandbox is a path plus a generated profile string).

tx is the sending half of the update channel — every spawned task gets a clone.

fetcher is its own reqwest::Client, deliberately not the OpenRouter one. Two reasons: a separate connection pool means a vetted connection is never shared across a trust boundary, and the client carrying your API key is never pointed at a URL the model chose.

65 
66/// Shared context the event handlers need to start new background work.
67struct Ctx {
68 client: Client,
69 sandbox: Sandbox,
70 /// Its own HTTP client, never the OpenRouter one: a separate connection pool
71 /// keeps a vetted connection from being shared across a trust boundary, and
72 /// the API-key-bearing client is never pointed at a model-chosen URL.
73 fetcher: Fetcher,
74 timeout: Duration,
75 tx: mpsc::Sender<Tagged>,
76}

fn main — build everything before taking the terminal

L77–L94

Four things happen in a deliberate order.

  • dotenvy::dotenv() first, so a .env file can supply OPENROUTER_API_KEY before Args::parse() reads environment-backed arguments.
  • The API key and the Sandbox are built before tui::init().
  • run(...) does the real work.
  • tui::restore() runs unconditionally, then the result is returned — so a failure inside run still leaves a usable terminal.
Why the ordering matters: once the alternate screen is active, anything printed to stdout vanishes when it is torn down. Constructing the sandbox first means "this platform is not macOS" prints as an ordinary error message instead of flashing invisibly.
77 
78#[tokio::main]
79async fn main() -> Result<()> {
80 // A .env in the working directory is convenient but entirely optional.
81 let _ = dotenvy::dotenv();
82 
83 let args = Args::parse();
84 let api_key = Args::api_key()?;
85 let client = Client::new(api_key, args.model.clone())?;
86 // Built before the terminal is taken over, so a sandbox failure prints
87 // normally instead of being swallowed by the alternate screen.
88 let sandbox = Sandbox::new(args.root()?)?;
89 
90 let terminal = tui::init()?;
91 let result = run(terminal, client, sandbox, args).await;
92 tui::restore();
93 result
94}

fn run — assembling App and the channel

L95–L132

App::new takes only the four things it genuinely cannot work without; everything else is assigned as a field right after. The comment on App::new explains the split — debug is toggleable at runtime via /debug, so it would be odd as a constructor argument.

app.debug = args.debug || cfg!(debug_assertions) means a cargo run (dev profile) starts in debug mode automatically, while a release build needs the flag.

The channel is bounded at 8. That bound is load-bearing during streaming: when the UI falls behind, tx.send().await blocks the task, which back-pressures the HTTP read, so tokens queue in the kernel socket buffer rather than being dropped.

95 
96async fn run(mut terminal: tui::Tui, client: Client, sandbox: Sandbox, args: Args) -> Result<()> {
97 let mut app = App::new(
98 client.model().to_string(),
99 args.system.clone(),
100 args.max_iterations.max(1),
101 args.sessions_dir.clone(),
102 );
103 app.debug = args.debug || cfg!(debug_assertions);
104 app.max_retries = args.max_retries;
105 // Reads resolve paths in-process against the sandbox root, so the app needs
106 // the sandbox itself, not just its root.
107 app.sandbox = Some(sandbox.clone());
108 app.confirm_reads = args.confirm_reads;
109 app.confirm_fetches = args.confirm_fetch;
110 app.price_in = args.price_in;
111 app.price_out = args.price_out;
112 app.push_notice(format!(
113 "Sandbox root: {} Type /help for commands.",
114 sandbox.root().display()
115 ));
116 
117 let mut events = EventStream::new();
118 let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::channel::<Tagged>(8);
119 let ctx = Ctx {
120 client,
121 sandbox,
122 // `Policy::strict` is the only policy production ever builds; the
123 // loosened one is `#[cfg(test)]` and does not exist in this binary.
124 fetcher: Fetcher::new(fetch::Policy::strict(args.timeout()))?,
125 timeout: args.timeout(),
126 tx,
127 };
128 // The current in-flight task, if any, so `Esc` can cancel it.
129 let mut inflight: Option<InFlight> = None;
130 let mut ticker = tokio::time::interval(TICK);
131 let mut metrics = ui::Metrics::default();
132 

the event loop — draw, select, autosave

L133–L173

The heart of the program. Read it as: draw first, then wait for whatever happens next.

terminal.draw returns ui::Metrics — geometry measured during rendering (where the Allow/Deny buttons landed, how tall the transcript is). That is how mouse hit-testing and page-scroll sizing get correct numbers without ui and main having to agree on layout maths separately.

The three select! arms are terminal input, background results, and the timer. The timer arm only bumps app.tick when the app is actually busy, so an idle session does not repaint 12 times a second for no reason — but the loop still wakes, which is why the arm is unconditional.

maybe_autosave() sits after the select! rather than inside any one arm, so it catches a settled turn no matter what caused it: a reply landing, a cancel, an error, or a /load.

133 loop {
134 terminal.draw(|frame| metrics = ui::draw(frame, &mut app))?;
135 
136 tokio::select! {
137 // Terminal input.
138 Some(event) = events.next() => {
139 match event {
140 Ok(event) => handle_event(event, &mut app, &ctx, &mut inflight, metrics),
141 // A read error means the terminal is gone; exit rather than spin.
142 Err(err) => {
143 app.push_error(format!("terminal input error: {err}"));
144 app.should_quit = true;
145 }
146 }
147 }
148 
149 // Background work finished.
150 Some(tagged) = rx.recv() => handle_update(tagged, &mut app, &ctx, &mut inflight),
151 
152 // Idle redraw, so the spinner animates while we wait.
153 _ = ticker.tick() => {
154 if matches!(
155 app.status,
156 app::Status::Waiting | app::Status::Streaming | app::Status::Running
157 ) {
158 app.tick = app.tick.wrapping_add(1);
159 }
160 }
161 }
162 
163 // Persist a completed turn. A cheap no-op unless the conversation just
164 // changed and settled back to idle, so it runs after replies, cancels,
165 // errors, and loads alike.
166 app.maybe_autosave();
167 
168 if app.should_quit {
169 return Ok(());
170 }
171 }
172}

fn handle_update — background results

L174–L236

The stale check is the first line, before the match: if the generation does not match, nothing else in this function runs.

Then note the pattern shared by every terminal arm: clear inflight (the task is done, there is nothing left to cancel), tell app, and if app hands back a Vec<Message>, immediately spawn the next request. That is the agentic loop — it is not a loop construct anywhere, it is this: a result comes back, App decides whether the conversation continues, and if so a new request goes out.

ReplyEnd(Ok) is the interesting case. The streamed text is thrown away (finish_stream) and the authoritative full text from the completion is committed through push_response instead. Streaming is display-only; parsing and approval happen once, on the whole reply.

The ReplyEnd arm now asks a second question. It used to be "did push_response give me messages? then send them." A None meant the loop pauses — idle, or waiting at the modal.

Why None is now a question rather than an answer: a fetch is auto-approved, so nothing is pending and nothing is idle — but it is network I/O, so App cannot run it inline the way it runs a read. It parks the URL instead, and take_pending_fetch is how the event loop finds out. This keeps every background task starting from the same place; the alternative was giving App the ability to spawn, which would have put tokio into the one file that has no I/O in it.

The Update::Fetch arm has no error branch, because Fetcher::fetch has no way to fail — the outcome carries the reason and goes straight back to the model, exactly like a command's non-zero exit.

174fn handle_update(tagged: Tagged, app: &mut App, ctx: &Ctx, inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>) {
175 // Drop anything from a task the user has since cancelled or superseded.
176 if tagged.generation != app.generation() {
177 return;
178 }
179 
180 match tagged.update {
181 // Live tokens accumulate in the display-only streaming buffer.
182 Update::Delta(delta) => app.push_delta(&delta),
183 // The reply is complete. Drop the live view and commit the full text
184 // through the normal path — a malformed reply earns a corrective retry,
185 // which comes back as messages to resend.
186 Update::ReplyEnd(Ok(completion)) => {
187 *inflight = None;
188 app.mark_request_done();
189 app.finish_stream();
190 match app.push_response(completion.content, completion.usage) {
191 Some(messages) => spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages),
192 // An auto-approved fetch is parked rather than returned, since
193 // it is background work the app layer cannot start itself.
194 None => {
195 if let Some(url) = app.take_pending_fetch() {
196 spawn_fetch(app, ctx, inflight, url);
197 }
198 }
199 }
200 }
201 Update::ReplyEnd(Err(message)) => {
202 *inflight = None;
203 app.mark_request_done();
204 app.finish_stream();
205 app.push_error(message);
206 }
207 // A finished command goes straight back to the model, continuing the loop.
208 Update::Command(Ok(output)) => {
209 *inflight = None;
210 let messages = app.push_command_result(output);
211 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
212 }
213 Update::Command(Err(message)) => {
214 *inflight = None;
215 app.push_error(format!("could not run command: {message}"));
216 }
217 // A finished write does the same — its result feeds the loop.
218 Update::Write(Ok(outcome)) => {
219 *inflight = None;
220 let messages = app.push_write_result(outcome);
221 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
222 }
223 Update::Write(Err(message)) => {
224 *inflight = None;
225 app.push_error(format!("could not write file: {message}"));
226 }
227 // A fetch always produces an outcome — a refused URL or an HTTP error is
228 // reported to the model as a result, so it can try something else.
229 Update::Fetch(outcome) => {
230 *inflight = None;
231 let messages = app.push_fetch_result(*outcome);
232 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
233 }
234 }
235}
236 

fn handle_event — keys, mouse, paste

L237–L291

Keys are delegated to handle_key. Everything else is here.

key.kind == KeyEventKind::Press matters on Windows terminals and under the kitty protocol, where release events are also delivered — without the guard every keystroke would register twice.

The mouse arms are ordered by modal precedence: approval buttons first, then the session picker, then plain scrolling. Both overlays handle hover (Moved) as well as click, so moving the mouse over Deny focuses it and a subsequent Enter does the same thing as clicking — keyboard and mouse never disagree about what is selected.

Paste is gated on !app.is_busy() and normalises CRLF, so pasting from a Windows-ish source does not leave stray carriage returns in the buffer.

237fn handle_event(
238 event: Event,
239 app: &mut App,
240 ctx: &Ctx,
241 inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>,
242 metrics: ui::Metrics,
243) {
244 match event {
245 Event::Key(key) if key.kind == KeyEventKind::Press => {
246 handle_key(key, app, ctx, inflight, metrics)
247 }
248 Event::Mouse(mouse) => match mouse.kind {
249 // Clicking a modal button is equivalent to confirming it.
250 MouseEventKind::Down(MouseButton::Left) if app.pending().is_some() => {
251 if ui::hit(metrics.allow_button, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
252 allow(app, ctx, inflight);
253 } else if ui::hit(metrics.deny_button, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
254 deny(app, ctx, inflight);
255 }
256 }
257 // Hovering a button focuses it, so click and keyboard agree.
258 MouseEventKind::Moved if app.pending().is_some() => {
259 if ui::hit(metrics.allow_button, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
260 app.set_choice(Choice::Allow);
261 } else if ui::hit(metrics.deny_button, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
262 app.set_choice(Choice::Deny);
263 }
264 }
265 // Clicking a session row loads it; hovering focuses it.
266 MouseEventKind::Down(MouseButton::Left) if app.picker().is_some() => {
267 if let Some(i) = picker_row_at(metrics, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
268 // Only load when the click lands on a real row.
269 if app.picker_select(i) {
270 app.picker_confirm();
271 }
272 }
273 }
274 MouseEventKind::Moved if app.picker().is_some() => {
275 if let Some(i) = picker_row_at(metrics, mouse.column, mouse.row) {
276 app.picker_select(i);
277 }
278 }
279 MouseEventKind::ScrollUp => app.scroll_up(3),
280 MouseEventKind::ScrollDown => app.scroll_down(3, metrics.max_scroll()),
281 _ => {}
282 },
283 Event::Paste(text) if !app.is_busy() && app.picker().is_none() => {
284 // Normalise line endings so pasted CRLF does not leave stray \r.
285 app.input
286 .insert_str(&text.replace("\r\n", "\n").replace('\r', "\n"));
287 }
288 _ => {}
289 }
290}

fn picker_row_at — mouse → list index

L292–L300

Turns a mouse position into a session-list index using the geometry captured during the last render. metrics.picker_offset is the list's scroll offset, so this works when the list is scrolled.

Returns None outside the list rectangle, which is what makes a click on the empty space below the last row do nothing rather than selecting whatever row the arithmetic happened to produce.

292/// Which session row a mouse position falls on, using the picker geometry from
293/// the last rendered frame. `None` when the point is outside the list.
294fn picker_row_at(metrics: ui::Metrics, column: u16, row: u16) -> Option<usize> {
295 let list = metrics.picker_list?;
296 if !ui::hit(Some(list), column, row) {
297 return None;
298 }
299 Some(metrics.picker_offset + (row - list.y) as usize)
300}

fn allow — approve and run

L301–L358

Three distinct paths out of an approval.

  • A Read needs no subprocess, so it is done inline and the loop continues immediately. This branch is only reachable under --confirm-reads; normally a read never becomes pending at all.
  • Shell and Write spawn a task.
  • Edit and Response are unreachable — an edit was already converted into a Write by App::approve, and a Response is never approvable.

The task construction is the standard shape used twice in this file: bump the generation, clone what the task needs, make a one-shot pair, tokio::spawn, store the sender in inflight.

Why the cancel future is built this way: let _ = cancel_rx.await; discards the result deliberately. Whether the sender sent or was dropped, the await resolves — both mean "stop", so both should interrupt the work.

The Fetch arm is only reachable under --confirm-fetch; without it a fetch never becomes pending in the first place. It returns early like the read arm does, but for the opposite reason: a read is done inline because it needs no task, while a fetch needs spawn_fetch — the shared spawn path, so the approved and auto-approved routes behave identically.

301 
302/// Approve the pending action and start running it — a shell command or a write.
303fn allow(app: &mut App, ctx: &Ctx, inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>) {
304 let Some(action) = app.approve() else { return };
305 
306 // A read needs no subprocess, so it is done inline and the loop continues
307 // immediately. Only reachable under `--confirm-reads`; otherwise a read
308 // never becomes pending in the first place.
309 let action = match action {
310 Action::Read { path } => {
311 let messages = app.perform_read(&path);
312 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
313 return;
314 }
315 // Only reachable under `--confirm-fetch`; otherwise the dispatch parks
316 // the fetch rather than making it pending.
317 Action::Fetch { url } => {
318 spawn_fetch(app, ctx, inflight, url);
319 return;
320 }
321 other => other,
322 };
323 
324 let generation = app.next_generation();
325 let sandbox = ctx.sandbox.clone();
326 let timeout = ctx.timeout;
327 let tx = ctx.tx.clone();
328 let (cancel_tx, cancel_rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
329 tokio::spawn(async move {
330 // The receiver resolves when the sender is used or dropped, either way
331 // interrupting the work.
332 let cancel = async {
333 let _ = cancel_rx.await;
334 };
335 let update = match action {
336 Action::Shell(command) => Update::Command(
337 exec::run_cancellable(&sandbox, &command, timeout, cancel)
338 .await
339 .map_err(|e| format!("{e:#}")),
340 ),
341 Action::Write { path, contents } => Update::Write(
342 exec::write_file(&sandbox, &path, &contents, timeout, cancel)
343 .await
344 .map_err(|e| format!("{e:#}")),
345 ),
346 // A Response is never approvable, a Read and a Fetch were handled
347 // above, and an Edit is converted to a Write by `approve`, so none
348 // are reachable.
349 Action::Read { .. }
350 | Action::Fetch { .. }
351 | Action::Edit { .. }
352 | Action::Response(_) => return,
353 };
354 let _ = tx.send(Tagged { generation, update }).await;
355 });
356 *inflight = Some(InFlight { cancel: cancel_tx });
357}
358 

fn deny — refuse and tell the model

L359–L364

Denial is not silence. app.deny() pushes an <ai-harness-denied> frame into the conversation and returns the messages to send, so the model finds out it was refused and can propose something else rather than assuming its command ran.

359/// Refuse the pending command and let the model know.
360fn deny(app: &mut App, ctx: &Ctx, inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>) {
361 if let Some(messages) = app.deny() {
362 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
363 }
364}

fn handle_key — modal precedence

L365–L427

The guards at the top of this function are the whole keyboard-focus model, in priority order.

  1. Ctrl+C always quits, even through a modal.
  2. Approval modal owns the keyboard while open, and returns — so stray typing cannot leak into the prompt hidden behind it. Note Esc here means Deny, not cancel-the-turn.
  3. Session picker likewise.
  4. Busy + Esc is the actual interrupt: signal the task, then app.cancel(), which bumps the generation.

Only after all four does ordinary editing get a look in.

365 
366fn handle_key(
367 key: KeyEvent,
368 app: &mut App,
369 ctx: &Ctx,
370 inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>,
371 metrics: ui::Metrics,
372) {
373 let ctrl = key.modifiers.contains(KeyModifiers::CONTROL);
374 let alt = key.modifiers.contains(KeyModifiers::ALT);
375 let shift = key.modifiers.contains(KeyModifiers::SHIFT);
376 let max_scroll = metrics.max_scroll();
377 let page = metrics.transcript_height.saturating_sub(1).max(1);
378 
379 // Ctrl+C always quits, even with the modal up.
380 if ctrl && key.code == KeyCode::Char('c') {
381 app.should_quit = true;
382 return;
383 }
384 
385 // The approval modal owns the keyboard while it is open, so stray typing
386 // cannot leak into the prompt hidden behind it. Esc here means Deny (refuse
387 // this command, continue the loop), not cancel-the-turn.
388 if app.pending().is_some() {
389 match key.code {
390 KeyCode::Left | KeyCode::Right | KeyCode::Tab | KeyCode::BackTab => app.toggle_choice(),
391 KeyCode::Char('y') | KeyCode::Char('Y') => allow(app, ctx, inflight),
392 KeyCode::Char('n') | KeyCode::Char('N') | KeyCode::Esc => deny(app, ctx, inflight),
393 KeyCode::Enter => match app.pending().map(|p| p.selected) {
394 Some(Choice::Allow) => allow(app, ctx, inflight),
395 Some(Choice::Deny) => deny(app, ctx, inflight),
396 None => {}
397 },
398 KeyCode::PageUp => app.scroll_up(page),
399 KeyCode::PageDown => app.scroll_down(page, max_scroll),
400 _ => {}
401 }
402 return;
403 }
404 
405 // The session picker owns the keyboard while it is open.
406 if app.picker().is_some() {
407 match key.code {
408 KeyCode::Up => app.picker_move(-1),
409 KeyCode::Down => app.picker_move(1),
410 KeyCode::PageUp => app.picker_move(-(page as isize)),
411 KeyCode::PageDown => app.picker_move(page as isize),
412 KeyCode::Enter => app.picker_confirm(),
413 KeyCode::Esc => app.picker_cancel(),
414 _ => {}
415 }
416 return;
417 }
418 
419 // While a stream or command is in flight (no modal), Esc interrupts it.
420 if app.is_busy() && key.code == KeyCode::Esc {
421 if let Some(handle) = inflight.take() {
422 let _ = handle.cancel.send(());
423 }
424 app.cancel();
425 return;
426 }
427 

fn handle_key — the main match

L428–L495

Ordered by specificity, since match takes the first arm that fits. Two groups are worth noticing.

The completion-menu arms (Tab, Up, Down, BackTab) are all guarded on !app.completions().is_empty(). That guard is why Tab still inserts four spaces and ↑ still recalls history the rest of the time — these keys only bind while the menu is actually open.

_ if app.is_busy() => {} at line 426 is a wall: every arm below it is editing, and editing is frozen while work is in flight. Everything above it (scrolling, submit, quit) still works while busy.

KeyCode::Enter calls accept_completion() before submit(), which is why typing /de and pressing Enter runs /debug without completing first.

428 match key.code {
429 // --- Global ---
430 KeyCode::Char('d') if ctrl && app.input.is_blank() => app.should_quit = true,
431 
432 // --- Scrolling ---
433 KeyCode::PageUp => app.scroll_up(page),
434 KeyCode::PageDown => app.scroll_down(page, max_scroll),
435 KeyCode::Up if ctrl || alt => app.scroll_up(1),
436 KeyCode::Down if ctrl || alt => app.scroll_down(1, max_scroll),
437 
438 // --- Submit / newline ---
439 // Alt+Enter always works. Shift+Enter only reaches us on terminals that
440 // support the kitty keyboard protocol, so it is a bonus, not the path.
441 KeyCode::Enter if alt || shift => app.input.insert_char('\n'),
442 // --- Completion menu ---
443 // These only bind while the menu is open, so Tab still indents and
444 // Up/Down still scroll the rest of the time.
445 KeyCode::Tab if !app.completions().is_empty() => {
446 app.accept_completion();
447 }
448 KeyCode::Down if !app.completions().is_empty() => app.move_completion(1),
449 KeyCode::Up if !app.completions().is_empty() => app.move_completion(-1),
450 KeyCode::BackTab if !app.completions().is_empty() => app.move_completion(-1),
451 
452 // `submit` handles slash commands locally and returns `None` for them,
453 // so nothing typed as a command reaches the model.
454 KeyCode::Enter => {
455 // Enter runs the highlighted command, so a partially-typed name
456 // does not need completing first.
457 app.accept_completion();
458 if let Some(messages) = app.submit() {
459 spawn_request(app, ctx, inflight, messages);
460 }
461 }
462 
463 _ if app.is_busy() => {} // editing is frozen while work is in flight
464 
465 // --- Editing ---
466 KeyCode::Char('l') if ctrl => app.reset_conversation(),
467 KeyCode::Char('u') if ctrl => app.input.delete_to_line_start(),
468 KeyCode::Char('w') if ctrl => app.input.delete_word_before(),
469 KeyCode::Char('a') if ctrl => app.input.move_to_line_start(),
470 KeyCode::Char('e') if ctrl => app.input.move_to_line_end(),
471 KeyCode::Char('k') if ctrl => app.input.clear(),
472 KeyCode::Backspace if alt || ctrl => app.input.delete_word_before(),
473 KeyCode::Backspace => app.input.backspace(),
474 KeyCode::Delete => app.input.delete(),
475 KeyCode::Left if alt || ctrl => app.input.move_word_left(),
476 KeyCode::Right if alt || ctrl => app.input.move_word_right(),
477 KeyCode::Left => app.input.move_left(),
478 KeyCode::Right => app.input.move_right(),
479 KeyCode::Home if ctrl => app.input.move_to_start(),
480 KeyCode::Home => app.input.move_to_line_start(),
481 KeyCode::End if ctrl => app.input.move_to_end(),
482 // End resumes following if the transcript is scrolled back, otherwise
483 // it does the ordinary line-end move.
484 KeyCode::End if !app.follow => app.scroll_to_bottom(max_scroll),
485 KeyCode::End => app.input.move_to_line_end(),
486 KeyCode::Tab => app.input.insert_str(" "),
487 // Prompt history recall. Bare Up/Down reach here only when not busy
488 // (above guard), not scrolling (Ctrl/Alt arms above), and with no
489 // completion menu open (an empty prompt has none).
490 KeyCode::Up => app.recall_prev(),
491 KeyCode::Down => app.recall_next(),
492 KeyCode::Char(c) if !ctrl => app.input.insert_char(c),
493 _ => {}
494 }
495}

spawn_fetch and spawn_request — starting background work

L496–L554

The other half of the spawn pattern. mark_request_sent() starts the clock that Ledger uses for "time spent waiting".

Note what happens on cancel: stream_reply returns None, so no terminal update is sent at all. That is belt and braces — the generation check would have dropped it anyway, but not sending is cheaper and clearer.

spawn_fetch is the same five-step shape as everything else that runs in the background: bump the generation, clone what the task needs, make a one-shot cancel channel, spawn, and store the handle so Esc can reach it. That is the whole cost of not being able to run a fetch inline.

496 
497/// Fetch a URL in the background.
498///
499/// Shared by the automatic path and the `--confirm-fetch` approval path. Unlike
500/// a read this cannot run inline: it is network I/O, so it needs the same
501/// generation tagging and cancel signal a command gets.
502fn spawn_fetch(app: &mut App, ctx: &Ctx, inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>, url: String) {
503 let generation = app.next_generation();
504 let fetcher = ctx.fetcher.clone();
505 let tx = ctx.tx.clone();
506 let (cancel_tx, cancel_rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
507 tokio::spawn(async move {
508 let cancel = async {
509 let _ = cancel_rx.await;
510 };
511 let outcome = fetcher.fetch(&url, cancel).await;
512 let _ = tx
513 .send(Tagged {
514 generation,
515 update: Update::Fetch(Box::new(outcome)),
516 })
517 .await;
518 });
519 *inflight = Some(InFlight { cancel: cancel_tx });
520}
521 
522fn spawn_request(
523 app: &mut App,
524 ctx: &Ctx,
525 inflight: &mut Option<InFlight>,
526 messages: Vec<Message>,
527) {
528 let generation = app.next_generation();
529 app.mark_request_sent();
530 let client = ctx.client.clone();
531 let tx = ctx.tx.clone();
532 let (cancel_tx, cancel_rx) = oneshot::channel::<()>();
533 tokio::spawn(async move {
534 let cancel = async {
535 let _ = cancel_rx.await;
536 };
537 // A send failure just means the UI shut down; stop forwarding if so.
538 let end = match client.open_stream(&messages).await {
539 Ok(stream) => stream_reply(stream, &tx, generation, cancel).await,
540 Err(e) => Some(Err(format!("{e:#}"))),
541 };
542 // On cancel `end` is None, so we send nothing — the app has already
543 // moved on and any late update would be dropped as stale anyway.
544 if let Some(end) = end {
545 let _ = tx
546 .send(Tagged {
547 generation,
548 update: Update::ReplyEnd(end),
549 })
550 .await;
551 }
552 });
553 *inflight = Some(InFlight { cancel: cancel_tx });
554}

async fn stream_reply — the SSE pump

L555–L597

Consumes the event stream, forwarding each delta to the UI while accumulating the full text locally. The accumulated content is what gets parsed; the deltas are purely for the live display.

biased; in the select! is deliberate: without it, tokio picks a ready arm at random, so a fast stream could starve the cancel arm and Esc would feel unresponsive. With it, cancellation is checked first on every iteration.

tx.send(...).await — not try_send — is what creates the back-pressure described up in run. If the UI is slow, this task waits, and the HTTP body stops being read.

None => return Some(Ok(Completion { content, usage })) is the normal exit: the stream ended, hand back everything accumulated.

555 
556/// Forward stream deltas to the UI, accumulating the full reply.
557///
558/// Returns `Some(reply-or-error)` normally, or `None` if `cancel` fired — in
559/// which case the caller sends no terminal update.
560async fn stream_reply(
561 stream: impl futures_util::Stream<Item = anyhow::Result<openrouter::StreamEvent>>,
562 tx: &mpsc::Sender<Tagged>,
563 generation: u64,
564 cancel: impl std::future::Future<Output = ()>,
565) -> Option<Result<Completion, String>> {
566 use openrouter::StreamEvent;
567 futures_util::pin_mut!(stream);
568 tokio::pin!(cancel);
569 
570 let mut content = String::new();
571 let mut usage = None;
572 loop {
573 tokio::select! {
574 // Interrupt takes priority so a fast stream cannot starve it.
575 biased;
576 _ = &mut cancel => return None,
577 event = stream.next() => match event {
578 Some(Ok(StreamEvent::Delta(delta))) => {
579 content.push_str(&delta);
580 // `send().await` back-pressures the HTTP read, so tokens are
581 // never dropped when the UI falls behind.
582 if tx
583 .send(Tagged { generation, update: Update::Delta(delta) })
584 .await
585 .is_err()
586 {
587 return Some(Err("UI closed".to_string()));
588 }
589 }
590 Some(Ok(StreamEvent::Done { usage: Some(u) })) => usage = Some(u),
591 Some(Ok(StreamEvent::Done { usage: None })) => {}
592 Some(Err(e)) => return Some(Err(format!("{e:#}"))),
593 None => return Some(Ok(Completion { content, usage })),
594 },
595 }
596 }
597}

103 lines of code

The clap argument struct, plus the two lookups (working directory, API key) that need real logic.

uses app (for DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES)

used by main

Almost entirely declarative. Every flag is also readable from an environment variable, which is what makes OPENROUTER_MODEL=... cargo run work identically to cargo run -- --model ....

Read the doc comments as documentation in the literal sense: clap turns each one into the --help text, so they are the user-facing copy.

imports

L1–L8

Small surface. anyhow::Context is here for exactly one use — attaching the "here is how to fix it" message to a missing API key.

1//! CLI arguments and environment configuration.
2 
3use std::path::PathBuf;
4use std::time::Duration;
5 
6use anyhow::{Context, Result};
7use clap::Parser;
8 

const DEFAULT_MODEL

L9–L10

The model used when nothing is specified. A single &str, not a table — the harness deliberately knows nothing about which models exist.

9pub const DEFAULT_MODEL: &str = "z-ai/glm-5.2";
10 

struct Args — clap derive and --model

L11–L20

#[derive(Parser)] plus #[command(...)] generate the entire CLI. version with no value pulls the version from Cargo.toml.

The pattern every field below follows: short/long for the flag spelling, env for the environment fallback, and default_value when there is a sensible one. Precedence is clap's standard: explicit flag > environment variable > default.

11#[derive(Debug, Parser)]
12#[command(
13 name = "ai-harness",
14 version,
15 about = "A terminal harness for chatting with models via OpenRouter"
16)]
17pub struct Args {
18 /// OpenRouter model slug, e.g. `z-ai/glm-5.2` or `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.5`.
19 #[arg(short, long, env = "OPENROUTER_MODEL", default_value = DEFAULT_MODEL)]
20 pub model: String,

--system, --workdir, --command-timeout

L21–L32

system is appended to the protocol contract, never a replacement for it — see protocol::system_prompt, which takes it as Option<&str> and concatenates.

workdir is the sandbox root; None means "current directory", resolved by root() below.

21 
22 /// Extra guidance appended to the protocol system prompt (which is always sent).
23 #[arg(short, long, env = "AI_HARNESS_SYSTEM_PROMPT")]
24 pub system: Option<String>,
25 
26 /// Sandbox root. Commands run here and cannot write outside it.
27 #[arg(short, long, env = "AI_HARNESS_WORKDIR")]
28 pub workdir: Option<PathBuf>,
29 
30 /// Seconds before a command is killed.
31 #[arg(long, default_value_t = 30, env = "AI_HARNESS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT")]
32 pub command_timeout: u64,

--max-iterations, --confirm-reads, --confirm-fetch

L33–L54

The default of 100 round-trips is generous on purpose, and the doc comment says why: reads consume a round-trip like any other action, so a model that looks at six files before doing anything has already spent six.

confirm_reads is a bool with no default_value_t, which in clap means a bare presence flag.

--confirm-fetch is a separate flag from --confirm-reads rather than one "confirm the free things" switch, because the two risks are not the same one. A read is confined to the working directory; a fetch is an outbound request to a host the model chose. Someone can reasonably want the second behind a modal and not the first.

The doc comment is unusually long for a flag, and deliberately so: it says what turning it on buys, and — more importantly — states plainly what the address rules do not cover, so nobody has to infer it.

33 
34 /// Maximum model round-trips per prompt, bounding the agentic loop.
35 ///
36 /// Reads consume a round-trip like any other action, so this has to leave
37 /// room for gathering context as well as doing the work.
38 #[arg(long, default_value_t = 100, env = "AI_HARNESS_MAX_ITERATIONS")]
39 pub max_iterations: usize,
40 
41 /// Ask before each file read. Off by default: a read mutates nothing and
42 /// cannot leave the working directory, so it runs without interrupting you.
43 #[arg(long, env = "AI_HARNESS_CONFIRM_READS")]
44 pub confirm_reads: bool,
45 
46 /// Ask before each URL fetch. Off by default, like reads.
47 ///
48 /// Turn it on to keep the network step under approval: an auto-approved
49 /// read followed by an auto-approved fetch can move file contents off the
50 /// machine without asking, and the https-only, no-private-addresses rules
51 /// do not prevent that — they only stop a fetch reaching this machine or
52 /// this network.
53 #[arg(long, env = "AI_HARNESS_CONFIRM_FETCH")]
54 pub confirm_fetch: bool,

--debug, --max-retries, --sessions-dir

L55–L69

--debug only forces debug on; main also ORs it with cfg!(debug_assertions), so dev builds get it for free.

max_retries defaults to app::DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES rather than a literal, so the constant has exactly one definition even though it is referenced from two modules.

55 
56 /// Start with debug mode on, showing raw protocol frames. Toggle with /debug.
57 ///
58 /// Also enabled by default in non-shipping (`dev`) builds; the flag forces it on
59 /// even in release builds.
60 #[arg(long, env = "AI_HARNESS_DEBUG")]
61 pub debug: bool,
62 
63 /// Corrective retries allowed when a reply breaks the protocol.
64 #[arg(long, default_value_t = crate::app::DEFAULT_MAX_RETRIES, env = "AI_HARNESS_MAX_RETRIES")]
65 pub max_retries: usize,
66 
67 /// Directory for `/save` and `/load` session files.
68 #[arg(long, default_value = "sessions", env = "AI_HARNESS_SESSIONS_DIR")]
69 pub sessions_dir: PathBuf,

--price-in and --price-out

L70–L82

Both are Option<f64> and both must be set before any dollar figure appears (Ledger enforces the pairing). The reasoning is in the doc comment: input and output rates differ several-fold, so a number derived from only one of them would not be an estimate, it would be wrong.

Why prices are not built in: a hardcoded price table would go stale silently. Making the operator supply the rates means a wrong number is at least a number someone typed.
70 
71 /// Input price in dollars per million tokens, for the `/cost` estimate.
72 ///
73 /// Rates differ per model and change over time, so they are supplied rather
74 /// than baked in — a hardcoded table would go stale without anyone noticing.
75 /// Both this and `--price-out` must be set for a cost figure to appear.
76 #[arg(long, env = "AI_HARNESS_PRICE_IN")]
77 pub price_in: Option<f64>,
78 
79 /// Output price in dollars per million tokens. See `--price-in`.
80 #[arg(long, env = "AI_HARNESS_PRICE_OUT")]
81 pub price_out: Option<f64>,
82}

fn timeout and fn root

L83–L95

timeout clamps with .max(1) so --command-timeout 0 cannot mean "kill instantly".

root falls back to current_dir(). Note that it returns the path unresolved — canonicalisation happens in Sandbox::new, which is where it matters.

83 
84impl Args {
85 pub fn timeout(&self) -> Duration {
86 Duration::from_secs(self.command_timeout.max(1))
87 }
88 
89 /// Sandbox root, defaulting to the current directory.
90 pub fn root(&self) -> Result<PathBuf> {
91 match &self.workdir {
92 Some(dir) => Ok(dir.clone()),
93 None => std::env::current_dir().context("resolving the current directory"),
94 }
95 }

fn api_key — the one message worth writing carefully

L96–L113

An associated function, not a method: the key never lives in Args, so nothing that debug-prints the config can leak it.

The and_then catches the annoying case that std::env::var treats as success — the variable is set but empty, which otherwise produces a confusing 401 from OpenRouter several steps later.

96 
97 /// Read the API key from the environment, with a message that says how to fix it.
98 pub fn api_key() -> Result<String> {
99 std::env::var("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")
100 .context(
101 "OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set.\n\
102 Get a key at https://openrouter.ai/keys, then either export it:\n\
103 \n export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...\n\n\
104 or put it in a .env file next to the binary.",
105 )
106 .and_then(|key| {
107 if key.trim().is_empty() {
108 anyhow::bail!("OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set but empty");
109 }
110 Ok(key)
111 })
112 }
113}

tui.rs

85 lines of code

Terminal setup and teardown: raw mode, alternate screen, mouse capture, bracketed paste, and the kitty keyboard protocol.

uses crossterm, ratatui

used by main

The smallest file in the crate, and the one with the most "if this is wrong your shell is broken after quitting" risk. Its whole job is to make sure everything init turns on, restore turns back off — including after a panic.

The module doc explains why it exists at all rather than just calling ratatui::init: that helper only does raw mode and the alternate screen, and this program also needs mouse capture, bracketed paste, and enhanced keys.

module doc, imports, and the Tui alias

L1–L23

pub type Tui is the concrete terminal type, aliased once so main's signatures do not have to spell out Terminal<CrosstermBackend<Stdout>>.

The three capabilities beyond ratatui's defaults, and what each buys: mouse capture gives wheel scrolling and clickable modal buttons, bracketed paste makes a multi-line paste arrive as one Event::Paste instead of a burst of keystrokes (which would otherwise submit at the first newline), and the kitty protocol is what lets Shift+Enter be distinguished from Enter.

1//! Terminal setup and teardown.
2//!
3//! `ratatui::init` only enables raw mode and the alternate screen. We also want
4//! mouse capture (scrollback), bracketed paste (multi-line pastes arrive as one
5//! event), and — where supported — the kitty keyboard protocol, which is what
6//! makes Shift+Enter distinguishable from Enter.
7 
8use std::io::{Stdout, stdout};
9 
10use anyhow::{Context, Result};
11use crossterm::event::{
12 DisableBracketedPaste, DisableMouseCapture, EnableBracketedPaste, EnableMouseCapture,
13 KeyboardEnhancementFlags, PopKeyboardEnhancementFlags, PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags,
14};
15use crossterm::execute;
16use crossterm::terminal::{
17 EnterAlternateScreen, LeaveAlternateScreen, disable_raw_mode, enable_raw_mode,
18 supports_keyboard_enhancement,
19};
20use ratatui::backend::CrosstermBackend;
21use ratatui::{Terminal, TerminalOptions, Viewport};
22 
23pub type Tui = Terminal<CrosstermBackend<Stdout>>;

static ENHANCED_KEYS

L24–L27

An AtomicBool recording whether the kitty flags were actually pushed, so teardown knows whether there is anything to pop.

Why a static rather than a field: the panic hook needs to reach it, and a panic hook is a 'static closure that cannot borrow local state.
24 
25/// Whether the kitty keyboard protocol was pushed, so teardown knows to pop it.
26static ENHANCED_KEYS: std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool = std::sync::atomic::AtomicBool::new(false);
27 

fn init — raw mode and the screen

L28–L36

Raw mode first (so keystrokes arrive unbuffered and unechoed), then the three execute! escape sequences in one call.

EnterAlternateScreen is why quitting restores your shell scrollback untouched — the whole session runs on a separate screen buffer.

28pub fn init() -> Result<Tui> {
29 enable_raw_mode().context("enabling raw mode")?;
30 execute!(
31 stdout(),
32 EnterAlternateScreen,
33 EnableMouseCapture,
34 EnableBracketedPaste
35 )
36 .context("initialising terminal")?;

fn init — optional kitty keyboard protocol

L37–L48

Best-effort, guarded twice: supports_keyboard_enhancement() may fail to answer (hence .unwrap_or(false)), and the push itself may fail. Only if both succeed is the flag recorded.

DISAMBIGUATE_ESCAPE_CODES is the specific capability wanted — it makes modified keys report their modifiers, so Shift+Enter stops looking exactly like Enter.

Because it is optional, Alt+Enter is the documented way to insert a newline; Shift+Enter is a bonus on terminals that support it.

37 
38 // Optional: without it Shift+Enter is indistinguishable from Enter, which
39 // is why Alt+Enter is the documented way to insert a newline.
40 if supports_keyboard_enhancement().unwrap_or(false)
41 && execute!(
42 stdout(),
43 PushKeyboardEnhancementFlags(KeyboardEnhancementFlags::DISAMBIGUATE_ESCAPE_CODES)
44 )
45 .is_ok()
46 {
47 ENHANCED_KEYS.store(true, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::SeqCst);
48 }

fn init — panic hook and the Terminal

L49–L61

fn restore — undo everything, twice-safe

L62–L75

swap(false, ...) both reads and clears the flag atomically, which is what makes calling restore more than once harmless: the second call sees false and skips the pop. That matters because main calls it on the normal path and the panic hook calls it on the failure path.

Every result is discarded with let _ =. There is nothing sensible to do if restoring fails, and returning early would skip the remaining restoration steps — the ordering (pop keys, disable paste/mouse, leave alt screen, disable raw mode) is the exact reverse of init.

62 
63/// Undo everything [`init`] did. Safe to call more than once.
64pub fn restore() {
65 if ENHANCED_KEYS.swap(false, std::sync::atomic::Ordering::SeqCst) {
66 let _ = execute!(stdout(), PopKeyboardEnhancementFlags);
67 }
68 let _ = execute!(
69 stdout(),
70 DisableBracketedPaste,
71 DisableMouseCapture,
72 LeaveAlternateScreen
73 );
74 let _ = disable_raw_mode();
75}

fn set_panic_hook

L76–L85

Wraps the existing hook rather than replacing it: restore the terminal first, then call whatever hook was already installed, so the panic message prints onto a normal screen in normal cooked mode where you can actually read it.

Without this, a panic leaves you on the alternate screen in raw mode with the mouse captured — the message scrolls past invisibly and the shell appears hung.

76 
77/// Restore the terminal before a panic prints, so the message is readable and
78/// the shell is not left in raw mode with the mouse captured.
79fn set_panic_hook() {
80 let previous = std::panic::take_hook();
81 std::panic::set_hook(Box::new(move |info| {
82 restore();
83 previous(info);
84 }));
85}

protocol.rs

661 lines of code · 648 lines of tests

The wire contract: the tag vocabulary, the system prompt that teaches it, the encoders that frame results, and the strict parser that validates replies.

uses exec::CommandOutput, files::ReadOutcome

used by app, main

The most important file in the crate. Everything else serves the contract defined here: the model may reply with exactly one of six XML elements and nothing else.

The design conviction is in the last paragraph of the module doc: parsing is deliberately strict. A reply that is nearly right — prose around the tag, a markdown fence, two elements — is rejected rather than guessed at. Being lenient would mean protocol drift silently changing behaviour; being strict means it surfaces immediately, and the retry loop in app.rs hands the model a targeted correction.

The file has four parts, in this order: the vocabulary (tag constants, Action, ProtocolError), the encoders (harness → model framing), the parser (model → harness validation), and the system prompt — 120 lines of prose that is, functionally, the other half of the parser.

Note the direction split in the tag list: *-result tags are harness → model only and are never parsed as a reply, which is why REPLY_TAGS holds only six of the thirteen constants.

module doc — the contract in brief

L1–L35

Worth reading in full; it is the shortest correct statement of what this program is.

The final paragraph is the load-bearing one. "Rejected rather than guessed at" is a choice with a cost — more retries — bought for a benefit: you find out immediately when a model stops following the format, instead of discovering it through subtly wrong behaviour weeks later.

1//! The wire protocol between the harness and the model.
2//!
3//! User input goes out wrapped in `<ai-harness-query>`. The model must reply
4//! with exactly one recognised element and nothing else:
5//!
6//! ```text
7//! <ai-harness-shell>ls -la</ai-harness-shell>
8//! <ai-harness-response>All done.</ai-harness-response>
9//! ```
10//!
11//! After a shell action runs, the harness reports the outcome back to the
12//! model wrapped in `<ai-harness-shell-result>`:
13//!
14//! ```text
15//! <ai-harness-shell-result>
16//! exit code: 0
17//! stdout:
18//! ...
19//! stderr:
20//! ...
21//! </ai-harness-shell-result>
22//! ```
23//!
24//! This is harness → model only; it is never parsed as a model reply.
25//!
26//! Parsing is deliberately strict. A reply that is *nearly* right — prose around
27//! the tag, a code fence, two elements — is rejected rather than guessed at, so
28//! protocol drift shows up immediately instead of silently changing behaviour.
29

31 
32use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

the tag vocabulary

L36–L72

Thirteen constants, and they divide by direction:

  • Model → harness: read, fetch, shell, write, edit, response — the six in REPLY_TAGS.
  • Children of edit: old, new — valid only nested inside an edit.
  • Harness → model only: query, and the four *-result tags. These are never parsed as a reply.

Read the comment on REPLY_TAGS: leaving old and new out of it is what makes a bare <ai-harness-old> at the top level correctly rejected as an unknown tag.

Why query is checked separately from unknown tags: a model echoing back <ai-harness-query> is a specific, recognisable confusion, and it earns its own error message that says "that tag belongs to the harness" rather than the generic "unknown tag". Why the array length is written out: [&str; 6] rather than an inferred slice means adding a tag without updating the list is a compile error. Three tests then iterate this array and assert every tag appears in the error text, in the correction, and in the system prompt — so a new element cannot be added and left undocumented.
36pub const QUERY_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-query";
37pub const SHELL_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-shell";
38pub const RESPONSE_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-response";
39/// A file read. Non-mutating, so it runs without the approval modal.
40pub const READ_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-read";
41/// A URL fetch. Like a read, it runs without the approval modal; what bounds it
42/// is the destination policy in [`crate::fetch`] rather than a filesystem root.
43pub const FETCH_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-fetch";
44/// A file write. Unlike shell/read/response, its opening tag carries a `file=`
45/// attribute.
46pub const WRITE_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-write";
47/// A targeted edit: replace one exact span of a file. Carries `file=` like write.
48pub const EDIT_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-edit";
49/// The span an edit replaces. A child of [`EDIT_TAG`], never valid on its own.
50pub const OLD_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-old";
51/// What an edit replaces the old span with. A child of [`EDIT_TAG`].
52pub const NEW_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-new";
53/// Harness → model only. Carries the outcome of a shell action; never parsed.
54pub const RESULT_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-shell-result";
55/// Harness → model only. Carries the outcome of a file write; never parsed.
56pub const WRITE_RESULT_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-write-result";
57/// Harness → model only. Carries the contents of a file read; never parsed.
58pub const READ_RESULT_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-read-result";
59/// Harness → model only. Carries the text of a fetched page; never parsed.
60pub const FETCH_RESULT_TAG: &str = "ai-harness-fetch-result";
61 
62/// Tags the model is allowed to reply with at the top level. The edit children
63/// ([`OLD_TAG`], [`NEW_TAG`]) are not here: they are only valid nested inside an
64/// edit, so at the top level they are correctly rejected as unknown.
65const REPLY_TAGS: [&str; 6] = [
66 READ_TAG,
67 FETCH_TAG,
68 SHELL_TAG,
69 WRITE_TAG,
70 EDIT_TAG,
71 RESPONSE_TAG,
72];

enum Action — a validated reply

L73–L108

The parser's output type, and the vocabulary the rest of the program speaks. Once you hold an Action, the reply is valid — there is no way to construct one otherwise.

Every variant is a proposal, not a done deed. The doc comments say so repeatedly: "Not executed yet", "Not written yet", "Not applied yet". Execution is main.rs's job, and only after approval.

body() exists for the UI: the transcript renders every action with one layout, so it needs a single "primary text" accessor. For an edit that is the old span — the thing being replaced.

Fetch carries a url and nothing else — the same shape as Read, and for the same reason: the element has exactly one datum. file= exists on write and edit only because those carry a path and content.

Why the URL is the body rather than an attribute: putting it in the body reuses machinery that already exists. The parser rejects an attribute on any tag that is not write or edit, so <ai-harness-fetch url=…> is a protocol error for free, rather than a second spelling that quietly works.
73 
74/// A validated model reply.
75#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
76pub enum Action {
77 /// A shell command the model wants run. Not executed yet.
78 Shell(String),
79 /// A file the model wants to see. Runs without approval; see [`crate::files`].
80 Read { path: String },
81 /// A URL the model wants to read. Runs without approval; see [`crate::fetch`].
82 Fetch { url: String },
83 /// A file the model wants written. Not written yet.
84 Write { path: String, contents: String },
85 /// A targeted replacement of one exact span in a file. Not applied yet; the
86 /// span is resolved into a full rewrite during pre-flight.
87 Edit {
88 path: String,
89 old: String,
90 new: String,
91 },
92 /// A terminating answer for the user.
93 Response(String),
94}
95 
96impl Action {
97 /// The primary text of the action (the command, the answer, the path, the
98 /// URL, the file contents, or — for an edit — the span being replaced).
99 pub fn body(&self) -> &str {
100 match self {
101 Self::Shell(s) | Self::Response(s) => s,
102 Self::Read { path } => path,
103 Self::Fetch { url } => url,
104 Self::Write { contents, .. } => contents,
105 Self::Edit { old, .. } => old,
106 }
107 }
108}

fn expected_tags

L109–L117

Renders the six reply tags as <a>, <b>, or <c> for error messages. Generated from REPLY_TAGS, so adding a seventh element updates every error message that lists them without anyone remembering to.

109 
110/// The reply tags, phrased for an error message: `<a>, <b>, or <c>`.
111fn expected_tags() -> String {
112 let names: Vec<String> = REPLY_TAGS.iter().map(|tag| format!("<{tag}>")).collect();
113 match names.split_last() {
114 Some((last, rest)) => format!("{}, or {last}", rest.join(", ")),
115 None => String::new(),
116 }
117}

enum ProtocolError — fourteen ways to be wrong

L118–L173

Each variant carries enough context to tell the model precisely what it did, and several exist purely to give a better message in a case that a coarser error would already have covered.

Three worth singling out:

  • DelimiterInBody — the body contains its own closing tag. Would otherwise surface as a baffling "trailing content".
  • ChildOutOfOrder — an edit gave <new> before <old>. Would otherwise say "missing <old>", which is technically true and completely unhelpful.
  • QueryTagFromModel — as described above.
The pattern: these are not error codes, they are instructions to a model that will read them. A retry costs a round-trip and real money, so the message being actionable is worth a variant.
118 
119/// Why a reply was rejected. Each carries enough detail to show the user what
120/// actually came back.
121#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
122pub enum ProtocolError {
123 Empty,
124 /// Reply did not begin with a tag.
125 NotATag {
126 found: String,
127 },
128 /// Opening tag was never closed with `>`.
129 UnterminatedOpenTag,
130 /// A tag we do not recognise.
131 UnknownTag {
132 tag: String,
133 },
134 /// The model used the query tag, which only the harness may send.
135 QueryTagFromModel,
136 /// Opening tag had no matching closing tag.
137 MissingClosingTag {
138 tag: String,
139 },
140 /// Content after the closing tag — prose, or a second element.
141 TrailingContent {
142 tag: String,
143 trailing: String,
144 },
145 /// A recognised tag with nothing inside it.
146 EmptyBody {
147 tag: String,
148 },
149 /// A `<ai-harness-write>` without a usable `file=` attribute.
150 MissingFileAttribute,
151 /// A shell/response tag carried an attribute it should not have.
152 UnexpectedAttribute {
153 tag: String,
154 attr: String,
155 },
156 /// A body contained its own closing tag, so the element could not be framed.
157 /// Distinguished from [`Self::TrailingContent`] to give an actionable hint.
158 DelimiterInBody {
159 tag: String,
160 },
161 /// An edit was missing one of its required `<old>`/`<new>` children.
162 MissingChildTag {
163 parent: String,
164 child: String,
165 },
166 /// Content sat between or after an edit's children where none is allowed.
167 UnexpectedChildContent {
168 parent: String,
169 found: String,
170 },
171 /// An edit gave `<new>` before `<old>`.
172 ChildOutOfOrder,
173}

impl Display for ProtocolError

L174–L232

Where the actual correction text lives. Read a couple of these as prompts rather than as diagnostics — MissingFileAttribute does not say "missing attribute", it shows the correct syntax inline.

DelimiterInBody goes furthest: it explains the parse failure and suggests the workaround (use a shell heredoc), because there is no way to express that content in this element and the model needs a route forward, not just a rejection.

snippet() bounds every echoed fragment, so a 40 KB malformed reply cannot blow up the correction message.

174 
175impl fmt::Display for ProtocolError {
176 fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter<'_>) -> fmt::Result {
177 match self {
178 Self::Empty => write!(f, "the model returned an empty reply"),
179 Self::NotATag { found } => write!(
180 f,
181 "reply must start with a tag, but began with: {}",
182 snippet(found)
183 ),
184 Self::UnterminatedOpenTag => {
185 write!(f, "the opening tag was never closed with '>'")
186 }
187 Self::UnknownTag { tag } => {
188 write!(f, "unknown tag <{tag}>; expected {}", expected_tags())
189 }
190 Self::QueryTagFromModel => write!(
191 f,
192 "<{QUERY_TAG}> is sent by the harness, not the model; expected {}",
193 expected_tags()
194 ),
195 Self::MissingClosingTag { tag } => {
196 write!(f, "missing closing </{tag}>")
197 }
198 Self::TrailingContent { tag, trailing } => write!(
199 f,
200 "unexpected content after </{tag}>: {}",
201 snippet(trailing)
202 ),
203 Self::EmptyBody { tag } => write!(f, "<{tag}> was empty"),
204 Self::MissingFileAttribute => write!(
205 f,
206 "<{WRITE_TAG}> needs a file path, e.g. <{WRITE_TAG} file=path/to/file>…</{WRITE_TAG}>"
207 ),
208 Self::UnexpectedAttribute { tag, attr } => write!(
209 f,
210 "<{tag}> does not take attributes, but had: {}",
211 snippet(attr)
212 ),
213 Self::DelimiterInBody { tag } => write!(
214 f,
215 "the contents of <{tag}> contain the literal text </{tag}>, which \
216 the parser reads as the end of the element. This element cannot \
217 carry that text; write the file with a shell heredoc instead"
218 ),
219 Self::MissingChildTag { parent, child } => {
220 write!(f, "<{parent}> must contain a <{child}>…</{child}> element")
221 }
222 Self::UnexpectedChildContent { parent, found } => write!(
223 f,
224 "<{parent}> may contain only <{OLD_TAG}> then <{NEW_TAG}>, but also had: {}",
225 snippet(found)
226 ),
227 Self::ChildOutOfOrder => {
228 write!(f, "<{EDIT_TAG}> must give <{OLD_TAG}> before <{NEW_TAG}>")
229 }
230 }
231 }
232}

The whole outbound framing for a user prompt: wrap the trimmed text in <ai-harness-query>. Input is never sent as free text — that symmetry is what makes the model's obligation to reply in a single element feel like a format rather than a request.

234impl std::error::Error for ProtocolError {}
235 
236/// Wrap user input for sending to the model.
237pub fn encode_query(text: &str) -> String {
