L157–L169

A resolved edit: the complete new file contents, ready to be written. Built before the approval modal.

This is the type that makes the edit flow honest. It is stored in app::Pending.edit_plan, and on approval App::approve turns it into Action::Write { path, contents: plan.updated }. The file is not re-read or re-matched after you approve — so the bytes that land are exactly the ones the diff showed you, with no window for the file to change in between.

157 
158/// A prepared edit: the whole file with one span replaced, ready to be written.
159///
160/// Built before the approval modal so a hopeless edit (no match, or ambiguous)
161/// never reaches the user — it goes straight back to the model to fix.
162#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
163pub struct EditPlan {
164 pub path: String,
165 /// The full new file contents, with the one match replaced.
166 pub updated: String,
167 pub old_len: usize,
168 pub new_len: usize,
169}

fn plan_edit — exact, unique, or rejected

L170–L211

Search-and-replace with a strict uniqueness rule, and the three-way match on the match count is the heart of it:

  • 0 matches → rejected, with instructions to re-read and copy exactly.
  • 1 match → an EditPlan.
  • n matches → rejected, asking for more surrounding context.
Why insist on exactly one: an ambiguous edit that silently picked the first match would corrupt files in a way that is very hard to notice. Refusing costs one round-trip and the model fixes it itself — you are never asked to approve an edit that cannot apply.

read_to_string, not the truncating read above, since the result is written back in full. The size guard runs on metadata() before reading, so a giant file is refused rather than slurped and then rejected.

Every error string is written as an instruction the model can act on, not a diagnostic — these go straight into the conversation.

170 
171/// Resolve an edit against the file on disk, replacing the single occurrence of
172/// `old` with `new`.
173///
174/// Reads the *whole* file (not the truncating [`read`]) because the result is
175/// written back in full — a truncated read would silently drop the tail. Every
176/// failure is a message the model can act on: the match must exist and be
177/// unique, and the fix for each case is spelled out.
178pub fn plan_edit(sandbox: &Sandbox, path: &str, old: &str, new: &str) -> Result<EditPlan, String> {
179 let resolved = resolve(sandbox, path)?;
180 if resolved.is_dir() {
181 return Err(format!("{path} is a directory, not a file"));
182 }
183 // Guard on size before reading, so a giant file is refused rather than slurped.
184 let len = std::fs::metadata(&resolved)
185 .map_err(|e| format!("{path}: {e}"))?
186 .len();
187 if len > MAX_EDIT_BYTES {
188 return Err(format!(
189 "{path} is too large to edit in place; change it with a shell command instead"
190 ));
191 }
192 let contents = std::fs::read_to_string(&resolved)
193 .map_err(|_| format!("{path} is not UTF-8 text and cannot be edited this way"))?;
194 
195 match contents.matches(old).count() {
196 0 => Err(format!(
197 "the text to replace was not found in {path}; re-read the file and copy \
198 the text exactly, including whitespace"
199 )),
200 1 => Ok(EditPlan {
201 path: path.to_string(),
202 updated: contents.replacen(old, new, 1),
203 old_len: old.len(),
204 new_len: new.len(),
205 }),
206 n => Err(format!(
207 "the text to replace appears {n} times in {path}; include more \
208 surrounding lines so it matches exactly one place"
209 )),
210 }
211}

What the tests cover

~240 lines against a real temporary directory. The escape cases are the point: ../secret, an absolute path outside the root, and — the one a string check would miss — a symlink inside the root pointing outside it, which is refused because the check runs on the canonicalised path.

Also covered: reading .env is denied, a binary file is rejected, a file over 64 KB comes back truncated, and plan_edit returns the right message for zero matches, one match, and many.

command.rs

166 lines of code · 175 lines of tests

Slash-command parsing, the command table, and the completion menu's data source.

uses nothing — pure, no imports

used by app, ui

Entirely pure: no imports at all, no I/O, no state. It classifies a line of text and describes what commands exist. App::run_command does the actual work.

The design commitment worth noting is in the module doc: commands are handled locally and never sent to the model. A typo'd command is reported back to you rather than forwarded — silently sending /dbeug to the model as a prompt is the worst available outcome.

COMMANDS is the single source of truth for both /help and the completion menu, so those can never disagree about what exists.

enum Command

L1–L29

One variant per command. The four session commands carry Option<String> because each has a meaningful no-argument behaviour — /load with no name opens the picker, /fork with no name generates one, /rename with no name reports usage.

Unknown(String) is a variant rather than a parse failure, which is what lets App::run_command report it as a notice. Read the comment on it — the alternative (forwarding to the model) is explicitly rejected.

1//! Slash commands, handled locally and never sent to the model.
2//!
3//! `parse` returns `None` for ordinary prompts so callers fall through to the
4//! normal submit path. A leading `//` escapes to a literal `/`, so a prompt can
5//! still begin with a slash.

10 /// Toggle protocol frame visibility.
11 Debug,
12 Help,
13 Clear,
14 Quit,
15 /// Save the session; `None` uses a generated name.
16 Save(Option<String>),
17 /// Load a saved session; `None` lists what is available.
18 Load(Option<String>),
19 /// Rename the current session's file; `None` reports usage.
20 Rename(Option<String>),
21 /// Branch the current conversation into a new session; `None` generates a name.
22 Fork(Option<String>),
23 /// Report cumulative token spend for the session.
24 Cost,

26 /// user rather than forwarded — silently sending a typo'd command to the
27 /// model is the worst available outcome.

29}

The two things a typed line can be. Prompt may differ from what was typed, because a leading // escape gets unwrapped to a single / here.

33pub enum Input {
34 /// Run this command locally.

fn parse — classify a line

L40–L72

Reads top to bottom as a precedence list.

  1. //foo → a prompt that literally starts with /foo. Checked first, or the / branch below would swallow it.
  2. No leading / → an ordinary prompt.
  3. Otherwise, split the name from its argument and look it up.

The argument split is rest[name.len()..].trim() — everything after the first whitespace run, trimmed — so /save my session gives the argument my session with the internal space intact.

Aliases live in the match arms ("help" | "h" | "?") rather than in COMMANDS. They work when typed but are not listed, which is the choice explained in the table's doc comment below.

Note the fall-through comment: a bare / produces an empty name and is reported as unknown, same as a typo.

40 
41/// Classify a line of input.
42pub fn parse(input: &str) -> Input {
43 let trimmed = input.trim();
44 
45 // `//foo` is an escape for a prompt that really does start with a slash.
46 if let Some(rest) = trimmed.strip_prefix("//") {
47 return Input::Prompt(format!("/{rest}"));
48 }
49 
50 let Some(rest) = trimmed.strip_prefix('/') else {
51 return Input::Prompt(input.trim_end().to_string());
52 };
53 
54 // Split the name from its argument (everything after the first whitespace).
55 let name = rest.split_whitespace().next().unwrap_or("");
56 let arg = rest[name.len()..].trim();
57 let arg = (!arg.is_empty()).then(|| arg.to_string());
58 
59 Input::Command(match name.to_ascii_lowercase().as_str() {
60 "debug" => Command::Debug,
61 "help" | "h" | "?" => Command::Help,
62 "clear" | "reset" => Command::Clear,
63 "quit" | "exit" | "q" => Command::Quit,
64 "save" => Command::Save(arg),
65 "load" => Command::Load(arg),
66 "rename" => Command::Rename(arg),
67 "fork" => Command::Fork(arg),
68 "cost" | "tokens" => Command::Cost,
69 // A bare "/" has no name; report it the same way as any unknown.
70 _ => Command::Unknown(name.to_string()),
71 })
72}

fn completion_prefix — when to show the menu

L123–L139

Returns the partial command name if the prompt currently holds one, and None otherwise — which is the signal that closes the menu.

Three ways to get None, and each corresponds to a moment when the menu stops being useful: a // escape (not a command at all), no leading slash (ordinary text), or any whitespace in the rest (the name is settled and an argument is being typed).

App::completions() calls this on every keystroke rather than caching, so the menu cannot drift out of step with the buffer.

123 
124/// The partial command name being typed, if the prompt currently holds one.
125///
126/// `None` once the name is settled — after a space, for a `//` escape, or for
127/// ordinary text — so the menu appears only while it is still useful.
128pub fn completion_prefix(input: &str) -> Option<&str> {
129 let trimmed = input.trim();
130 if trimmed.starts_with("//") {
131 return None;
132 }
133 let rest = trimmed.strip_prefix('/')?;
134 // Once an argument is being typed the command itself is decided.
135 if rest.chars().any(char::is_whitespace) {
136 return None;
137 }
138 Some(rest)
139}

fn matching

L140–L148

Prefix filter, case-insensitive. Returns &'static Spec references — the table is a const, so nothing is allocated or cloned per keystroke.

140 
141/// Commands whose name starts with `prefix`, case-insensitively.
142pub fn matching(prefix: &str) -> Vec<&'static Spec> {
143 let prefix = prefix.to_ascii_lowercase();
144 COMMANDS
145 .iter()
146 .filter(|spec| spec.name.starts_with(&prefix))
147 .collect()
148}

fn help_text

L149–L166

Generated from COMMANDS, with the name column padded to the longest name so the descriptions line up. The two trailing lines document the keys the menu binds, which is otherwise undiscoverable.

150/// Listing shown by `/help`, generated from [`COMMANDS`].
151pub fn help_text() -> String {
152 let width = COMMANDS.iter().map(|c| c.name.len()).max().unwrap_or(0);
153 let mut lines = vec!["Commands (handled locally, never sent to the model):".to_string()];
154 for spec in COMMANDS {
155 lines.push(format!(
156 " /{:<width$} {}",
157 spec.name,
158 spec.description,
159 width = width
160 ));
161 }
162 lines.push(String::new());
163 lines.push("Tab completes a command; ↑/↓ choose, Enter runs it.".to_string());
164 lines.push("Start a prompt with // to send text beginning with a slash.".to_string());
165 lines.join("\n")
166}

What the tests cover

174 lines of table-driven parsing cases: every command and alias, the // escape, argument splitting (including arguments with spaces), case-insensitivity, a bare /, and unknown names.

completion_prefix is tested at each boundary — empty prompt, /, partial name, name-plus-space (menu closes), and the // escape (no menu).

input.rs

230 lines of code · 110 lines of tests

The prompt buffer: a multi-line string with a grapheme-aware cursor, plus the layout that maps it to screen rows and a cursor cell.

uses wrap, unicode-segmentation, unicode-width

used by app, ui

Pure state, no I/O, no terminal knowledge. main.rs maps keys to method calls here; ui.rs asks for a Layout and draws it.

Everything is grapheme-aware rather than char-aware. Backspacing over an emoji or an accented character built from combining marks removes the whole visible unit, not one codepoint of it. The cursor is a byte offset that is always kept on a grapheme boundary.

The module doc names the reason wrapping is done here instead of being left to ratatui's Paragraph: the rendered cursor position must match the wrapped text. Wrap it yourself and you know exactly where the cursor landed.

struct Input and struct Layout

L1–L23

Input is two fields: the text, and a byte offset that is always on a grapheme boundary. That invariant is maintained by every method here, and it is what lets text.insert and replace_range be called without ever panicking on a bad slice.

Layout is the render-ready form: wrapped rows plus the cursor as a (row, column) cell pair.

L56–L86

backspace and delete both go through the boundary helpers, so they remove a whole grapheme. Both are no-ops at the ends (prev_boundary returns None), which is why neither needs a bounds check.

delete_word_before is Ctrl+W; delete_to_line_start is Ctrl+U. Both delegate the "where does that land" question to the helpers at the bottom of the file.

57 pub fn backspace(&mut self) {
58 if let Some(prev) = self.prev_boundary(self.cursor) {
59 self.text.replace_range(prev..self.cursor, "");
60 self.cursor = prev;
61 }
62 }
63 
64 pub fn delete(&mut self) {

66 self.text.replace_range(self.cursor..next, "");
67 }
68 }
69

71 pub fn delete_word_before(&mut self) {

76 }

fn layout — text to rows and a cursor cell

L123–L157

The one function here with real work in it. Two levels of line breaking: hard newlines first, then soft wrapping of each logical line via wrap::line.

consumed tracks the byte offset of the current logical line's start, incremented by 1 for each \n — that is what lets a global cursor offset be translated into an offset within the current line.

self.cursor >= line_start && self.cursor <= line_end uses <= on both ends deliberately: the cursor sitting at the very end of a line is a real position, and an exclusive bound would fail to place it.

The final if rows.is_empty() guarantees at least one row, so an empty prompt still has somewhere to draw the cursor.

123 
124 /// Lay the buffer out at `width` cells, soft-wrapping on word boundaries
125 /// and hard-wrapping words that are longer than a line.
126 pub fn layout(&self, width: u16) -> Layout {
127 let width = width.max(1) as usize;
128 let mut rows: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
129 let mut cursor = (0u16, 0u16);
130 
131 // Hard lines first; `split` keeps a trailing empty segment for "a\n".
132 let mut consumed = 0usize;
133 for (i, logical) in self.text.split('\n').enumerate() {
134 if i > 0 {
135 consumed += 1; // the '\n' itself
136 }
137 let start_row = rows.len();
138 let wrapped = wrap::line(logical, width);
139 
140 // Where does the cursor fall within this logical line?
141 let line_start = consumed;
142 let line_end = consumed + logical.len();
143 if self.cursor >= line_start && self.cursor <= line_end {
144 let offset = self.cursor - line_start;
145 let (r, c) = locate(&wrapped, offset);
146 cursor = ((start_row + r) as u16, c as u16);
147 }
148 
149 rows.extend(wrapped.into_iter().map(|r| r.text));
150 consumed = line_end;
151 }
152 
153 if rows.is_empty() {
154 rows.push(String::new());
155 }
156 Layout { rows, cursor }
157 }

the private helpers

L158–L218

The primitives everything above is built from.

prev_boundary/next_boundary use grapheme_indices(true) — the true means extended grapheme clusters, the definition that keeps emoji-with-modifier sequences together.

word_start_before is two loops, and the split is the standard editor behaviour: first skip whitespace immediately behind the cursor, then skip the word. That is why Ctrl+W at the end of "hello " deletes hello and not just the space.

word_end_after is the mirror image, using peekable() so it can look at a grapheme before deciding to consume it.

158 
159 fn prev_boundary(&self, at: usize) -> Option<usize> {
160 self.text[..at]
161 .grapheme_indices(true)
162 .next_back()
163 .map(|(i, _)| i)
164 }
165 
166 fn next_boundary(&self, at: usize) -> Option<usize> {
167 self.text[at..].graphemes(true).next().map(|g| at + g.len())
168 }
169 
170 fn line_start(&self, at: usize) -> usize {
171 self.text[..at].rfind('\n').map_or(0, |i| i + 1)
172 }
173 
174 fn line_end(&self, at: usize) -> usize {
175 self.text[at..]
176 .find('\n')
177 .map_or(self.text.len(), |i| at + i)
178 }
179 
180 fn word_start_before(&self, at: usize) -> usize {
181 let head = &self.text[..at];
182 let mut idx = at;
183 // Skip whitespace immediately before the cursor, then the word itself.
184 for (i, g) in head.grapheme_indices(true).rev() {
185 if g.chars().all(char::is_whitespace) {
186 idx = i;
187 } else {
188 break;
189 }
190 }
191 for (i, g) in self.text[..idx].grapheme_indices(true).rev() {
192 if g.chars().all(char::is_whitespace) {
193 break;
194 }
195 idx = i;
196 }
197 idx
198 }
199 
200 fn word_end_after(&self, at: usize) -> usize {
201 let mut idx = at;
202 let mut it = self.text[at..].grapheme_indices(true).peekable();
203 while let Some(&(i, g)) = it.peek() {
204 if g.chars().all(char::is_whitespace) {
205 idx = at + i + g.len();
206 it.next();
207 } else {
208 break;
209 }
210 }
211 for (i, g) in self.text[idx..].grapheme_indices(true) {
212 if g.chars().all(char::is_whitespace) {
213 return idx + i;
214 }
215 }
216 self.text.len()
217 }
218}

fn locate — offset to (row, column)

L219–L230

Given the wrapped rows of one logical line and a byte offset into it, find which row the offset lands on and how many cells across it is.

Iterating in reverse (.rev()) is the trick: the first row whose start is at or before the offset is the right one. Forward iteration would need lookahead to know where each row ends.

The column is .width(), not a byte or character count — a CJK character occupies two terminal cells, and the cursor has to land in the right one.

219 
220/// Map a byte offset within a logical line to (row, column) in its wrapped rows.
221fn locate(rows: &[wrap::Row], offset: usize) -> (usize, usize) {
222 for (i, row) in rows.iter().enumerate().rev() {
223 if offset >= row.start {
224 let within = (offset - row.start).min(row.text.len());
225 let col = row.text.get(..within).unwrap_or(&row.text).width();
226 return (i, col);
227 }
228 }
229 (0, 0)
230}

What the tests cover

109 lines covering the cursor invariants: insert and delete across multi-byte characters, word motions with runs of whitespace, line-start/line-end on a multi-line buffer, and layout placing the cursor correctly at a wrap boundary and at the very end of the text.

112 lines of code · 92 lines of tests

Word wrapping, shared by the prompt editor and the transcript.

uses unicode-segmentation, unicode-width

used by input, ui

The smallest piece of real algorithm in the crate. Both callers need wrapping they can reason about exactly: the editor to place the cursor, the transcript to know its rendered height for scroll clamping.

The module doc explains why ratatui's own wrapping is not used — Paragraph only exposes its wrapped height behind an unstable feature. So this wraps up front and hands ratatui text that already fits.

Correctness here means cells, not characters: a CJK character is two cells wide, and a combining mark is zero.

L1–L22

A wrapped row carries its text and the byte offset in the source line where it starts.

Why start exists: without it the editor could not map a cursor offset back to a screen position. It is the single field that makes this module usable by input.rs rather than just by the renderer — see input::locate, which searches on exactly this.

13pub struct Row {

fn line — the wrapping algorithm

L23–L86

One logical line (no \n) to a vector of rows. Read it via the four pieces of state: current is the row being built, pending is the word being accumulated, and the two widths track cells.

The core idea is pending: non-space graphemes are held back rather than appended, so when the row runs out of space the whole word can move to the next row intact. Whitespace commits the pending word (flush).

The overflow branch at line 45 has three cases, and they are genuinely distinct:

  • Row has content and a word is pending → break before the word and carry it down. The normal case.
  • Word longer than an entire row → hard-break it where we are.
  • A single grapheme wider than the whole row → give it its own row and continue. Degenerate, but a 1-cell-wide terminal must not loop forever.

The trailing condition at line 82 is subtle and the comment explains it: the overlong-grapheme path already pushed its row, so pushing again unconditionally would append a blank row and inflate the reported height — which would then break scroll clamping.

23 
24/// Wrap one logical line (no `\n`) to `width` cells.
25///
26/// Breaks at spaces where possible and hard-breaks words too long to fit.
27/// Always returns at least one row, so an empty line still occupies a row.
28pub fn line(text: &str, width: usize) -> Vec<Row> {
29 let width = width.max(1);
30 if text.is_empty() {
31 return vec![Row::new(String::new(), 0)];
32 }
33 
34 let mut rows: Vec<Row> = Vec::new();
35 let mut current = String::new();
36 let mut current_start = 0usize;
37 let mut current_width = 0usize;
38 // The word being built up. Held back so it can move to the next row whole.
39 let mut pending: Vec<(usize, &str, usize)> = Vec::new();
40 
41 for (i, grapheme) in text.grapheme_indices(true) {
42 let w = cell_width(grapheme);
43 let pending_width: usize = pending.iter().map(|(_, _, w)| *w).sum();
44 
45 if current_width + pending_width + w > width {
46 if !current.is_empty() && !pending.is_empty() {
47 // Break before the pending word and carry it to the next row.
48 let carry_start = pending[0].0;
49 rows.push(Row::new(std::mem::take(&mut current), current_start));
50 current_start = carry_start;
51 current_width = 0;
52 flush(&mut current, &mut current_width, &mut pending);
53 } else {
54 flush(&mut current, &mut current_width, &mut pending);
55 if current.is_empty() {
56 // One grapheme wider than the whole row; give it its own row.
57 rows.push(Row::new(grapheme.to_string(), i));
58 current_start = i + grapheme.len();
59 continue;
60 }
61 // A word longer than a row: hard-break it here.
62 rows.push(Row::new(std::mem::take(&mut current), current_start));
63 current_start = i;
64 current_width = 0;
65 }
66 }
67 
68 if grapheme == " " || grapheme == "\t" {
69 // Whitespace terminates the pending word, so commit it.
70 flush(&mut current, &mut current_width, &mut pending);
71 current.push_str(grapheme);
72 current_width += w;
73 } else {
74 pending.push((i, grapheme, w));
75 }
76 }
77 
78 flush(&mut current, &mut current_width, &mut pending);
79 // Only emit a trailing row if it holds something. The overlong-grapheme
80 // path above emits its row directly, which would otherwise leave a blank
81 // row here and inflate the rendered height.
82 if !current.is_empty() || rows.is_empty() {
83 rows.push(Row::new(current, current_start));
84 }
85 rows
86}

fn text — the multi-line convenience

L87–L94

Splits on \n, wraps each piece, flattens to plain strings. Drops the start offsets, because the transcript renderer only needs the text — it is input.rs that needs offsets, and it calls line directly.

87 
88/// Wrap text that may contain `\n`, returning the flattened rows.
89pub fn text(input: &str, width: usize) -> Vec<String> {
90 input
91 .split('\n')
92 .flat_map(|logical| line(logical, width).into_iter().map(|r| r.text))
93 .collect()
94}

fn flush

L95–L101

Moves the pending word into the current row. Takes &mut to both and uses drain(..), so the pending vector is emptied and reused rather than reallocated on every word.

95 
96fn flush(current: &mut String, current_width: &mut usize, pending: &mut Vec<(usize, &str, usize)>) {
97 for (_, grapheme, w) in pending.drain(..) {
98 current.push_str(grapheme);
99 *current_width += w;
100 }
101}

fn cell_width

L102–L112

A wrapper around UnicodeWidthStr::width with one adjustment: a grapheme that reports width 0 but is not a control character is treated as width 1.

Why: an unassigned or unrenderable codepoint reports 0, but the terminal will still print something for it and advance the cursor. Trusting the 0 would make the wrapped text and the real screen disagree, and the cursor would drift.
102 
103/// Display width of a grapheme, treating unknown/zero-width non-controls as 1
104/// so an unrenderable character still advances the cursor.
105fn cell_width(grapheme: &str) -> usize {
106 let w = grapheme.width();
107 if w == 0 && !grapheme.chars().all(char::is_control) {
108 1
109 } else {
110 w
111 }
112}

What the tests cover

91 lines, and they read as a specification: breaking at spaces, hard-breaking an overlong word, a single grapheme wider than the entire row, an empty line still occupying one row, and start offsets being correct on every row (which is what input::locate depends on).

Width handling is tested with CJK and combining characters rather than ASCII, since ASCII would pass even with the width logic removed.

Cumulative token accounting for a session, and the only place that knows how to turn tokens into dollars.

uses openrouter::Usage, serde

used by app, session, ui

The newest file in the crate (still untracked in git at the time of writing). The module doc states the gap it filled: per-turn usage was shown against each reply, but nothing added it up, so there was no way to see what a session had cost.

Four counters and some formatting. The design decision worth carrying: it will only produce a dollar figure when given prices, and only when given both. Rates differ per model and change over time, so a hardcoded table would go stale without anyone noticing.

The other one is waiting_ms — time with a request actually in flight, not wall-clock since the session began. A session that sat idle overnight would otherwise report a meaningless number.

struct Ledger

L1–L32

Four counters. u64 rather than the API's u32 because these accumulate across every request in a session.

Serialize/Deserialize because the ledger is written into the session file — see session::Session, where it was added after format version 1 without a version bump, relying on #[serde(default)] to stay compatible in both directions.

The doc comment on waiting_ms is the one to read; it explains why this is not wall-clock time.

1//! Cumulative token accounting for a session.
2//!
3//! The per-turn `Usage` the API returns is shown against each reply, but
4//! nothing added it up: there was no way to see what a session had cost in
5//! total. This module keeps the running totals, and is deliberately the only
6//! place that knows how to turn them into dollars — which it will only do when
7//! given prices, since rates change and a hardcoded table goes stale silently.
8 
9use std::time::Duration;
10 
11use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
12 
13use crate::openrouter::Usage;
14 
15/// Running totals for a session.
16///
17/// Serialised into the session file, so a reloaded session keeps its history of
18/// spend. Counts are `u64` rather than the API's `u32` because they accumulate
19/// across every request in a session.
20#[derive(Debug, Clone, Default, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
21pub struct Ledger {
22 pub prompt_tokens: u64,
23 pub completion_tokens: u64,
24 /// Model round-trips that reported usage.
25 pub requests: u64,
26 /// Milliseconds spent with a request actually in flight.
27 ///
28 /// Not wall-clock since the session began: a session that sat idle
29 /// overnight would report a meaningless number. Time spent waiting on the
30 /// model is the figure that means something.
31 pub waiting_ms: u64,
32}

record, add_wait, and the small accessors

L33–L54

record folds in one reply's usage. App::push_response calls it before validating the reply — deliberately, since a malformed reply cost real tokens too, and a retry loop that billed nothing would understate spend precisely when it is going wrong.

add_wait clamps with .min(u128::from(u64::MAX)) before the cast, so a nonsensical duration saturates instead of wrapping. It is called on every request end — including cancels and failures, because that time was really spent.

33 
34impl Ledger {
35 /// Fold in one reply's usage.
36 pub fn record(&mut self, usage: &Usage) {
37 self.prompt_tokens += u64::from(usage.prompt_tokens);
38 self.completion_tokens += u64::from(usage.completion_tokens);
39 self.requests += 1;
40 }
41 
42 /// Add time spent on a request. Cancelled and failed requests count too —
43 /// that time was really spent.
44 pub fn add_wait(&mut self, elapsed: Duration) {
45 self.waiting_ms += elapsed.as_millis().min(u128::from(u64::MAX)) as u64;
46 }
47 
48 pub fn total_tokens(&self) -> u64 {
49 self.prompt_tokens + self.completion_tokens
50 }
51 
52 pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool {
53 self.requests == 0
54 }

fn cost — the both-or-nothing rule

L55–L68

let (input, output) = (price_in?, price_out?); — two ? on one line is the entire pairing rule. Either price missing returns None.

Why both are required: input and output rates commonly differ by three to five times. A figure derived from only one of them would not be an imprecise estimate, it would be a wrong number presented as a real one.
55 
56 /// Estimated spend in dollars, given per-million-token prices.
57 ///
58 /// `None` unless **both** prices are supplied: input and output rates
59 /// differ several-fold, so a figure derived from one of them would not be
60 /// an estimate, it would be wrong.
61 pub fn cost(&self, price_in: Option<f64>, price_out: Option<f64>) -> Option<f64> {
62 let (input, output) = (price_in?, price_out?);
63 const PER: f64 = 1_000_000.0;
64 Some(
65 (self.prompt_tokens as f64 / PER) * input
66 + (self.completion_tokens as f64 / PER) * output,
67 )
68 }

status_line and report

L69–L111

Two renderings of the same data for two places. status_line is the compact status-bar form (36.7k tok $0.04); report is the multi-line /cost breakdown.

Note the different number formatters: the status bar uses compact because width is scarce, the report uses thousands because exactness is the point.

When prices are absent, report does not just omit the cost line — it tells you which flags to set. An empty ledger short-circuits with a plain sentence rather than a table of zeroes.

\x20 at the start of the format lines is an escaped space, needed because the \ line-continuation in a Rust string strips leading whitespace on the next line.

69 
70 /// A short indicator for the status bar, e.g. `36.7k tok $0.04`.
71 pub fn status_line(&self, price_in: Option<f64>, price_out: Option<f64>) -> String {
72 let mut text = format!("{} tok", compact(self.total_tokens()));
73 if let Some(cost) = self.cost(price_in, price_out) {
74 text.push_str(&format!(" {}", money(cost)));
75 }
76 text
77 }
78 
79 /// The multi-line breakdown `/cost` prints.
80 pub fn report(&self, price_in: Option<f64>, price_out: Option<f64>) -> String {
81 if self.is_empty() {
82 return "No model requests yet this session.".to_string();
83 }
84 let mut text = format!(
85 "Session totals\n\
86 \x20 requests {}\n\
87 \x20 input tokens {}\n\
88 \x20 output tokens {}\n\
89 \x20 total tokens {}\n\
90 \x20 time waiting {}",
91 self.requests,
92 thousands(self.prompt_tokens),
93 thousands(self.completion_tokens),
94 thousands(self.total_tokens()),
95 duration(self.waiting_ms),
96 );
97 match self.cost(price_in, price_out) {
98 Some(cost) => text.push_str(&format!(
99 "\n estimated cost {} (at ${}/M in, ${}/M out)",
100 money(cost),
101 price_in.unwrap_or(0.0),
102 price_out.unwrap_or(0.0)
103 )),
104 None => text.push_str(
105 "\n Set --price-in and --price-out (dollars per million tokens) \
106 for a cost estimate.",
107 ),
108 }
109 text
110 }
111}

fn compact

L112–L123

1234 → 1.2k, 1234567 → 1.23M.

It truncates rather than rounds, and the doc comment gives the reason: rounding would let 999,999 render as 1000.0k instead of crossing cleanly into M.

112 
113/// `1234` → `1.2k`, `1_234_567` → `1.23M`. For places where width is scarce.
114///
115/// Truncates rather than rounding, so a value just under a unit boundary cannot
116/// render as `1000.0k` instead of crossing to `M`.
117fn compact(n: u64) -> String {
118 match n {
119 0..=999 => n.to_string(),
120 1_000..=999_999 => format!("{}.{}k", n / 1_000, (n % 1_000) / 100),
121 _ => format!("{}.{:02}M", n / 1_000_000, (n % 1_000_000) / 10_000),
122 }
123}

fn thousands

L124–L136

Comma grouping. (digits.len() - i).is_multiple_of(3) counts remaining digits rather than consumed ones, which is what makes the grouping correct without needing to know the total length in advance or reverse the string.

124 
125/// `1234567` → `1,234,567`. For the report, where exactness is the point.
126fn thousands(n: u64) -> String {
127 let digits = n.to_string();
128 let mut out = String::with_capacity(digits.len() + digits.len() / 3);
129 for (i, c) in digits.chars().enumerate() {
130 if i > 0 && (digits.len() - i).is_multiple_of(3) {
131 out.push(',');
132 }
133 out.push(c);
134 }
135 out
136}

fn money

L137–L145

Four decimal places below a cent, two above.

Without the small-value branch, an actual session cost of $0.004 would render as $0.00 — indistinguishable from free, which is exactly the wrong impression when the number is meant to build a habit of noticing.

137 
138/// Dollars, with enough precision to be useful at small amounts.
139fn money(dollars: f64) -> String {
140 if dollars < 0.01 && dollars > 0.0 {
141 format!("${dollars:.4}")
142 } else {
143 format!("${dollars:.2}")
144 }
145}

fn duration

L146–L157

Two units at most: 1h 20m, 5m 3s, or 42s. Seconds alongside hours would be noise at that scale.

146 
147fn duration(ms: u64) -> String {
148 let total = ms / 1000;
149 let (h, m, s) = (total / 3600, (total % 3600) / 60, total % 60);
150 if h > 0 {
151 format!("{h}h {m}m")
152 } else if m > 0 {
153 format!("{m}m {s}s")
154 } else {
155 format!("{s}s")
156 }
157}

What the tests cover

134 lines. The formatters get the most attention because they have the most boundaries: compact at 999/1000 and 999_999/1_000_000, thousands on 1-, 3-, and 7-digit numbers, money either side of the $0.01 cutoff, and duration crossing the minute and hour marks.

cost is checked to return None when either price is missing — the pairing rule — and the accumulation is checked to survive a serialise/deserialise round-trip.

session.rs

159 lines of code · 217 lines of tests

Saving and loading conversations as JSON files, plus the name sanitiser that keeps session names from escaping the directory.

uses app::Entry, ledger, openrouter::Message, serde_json

used by app

All file I/O, no state. App owns the current session name and decides when to save; this module knows how.

The thing to understand is what gets saved: both the model conversation (history, needed to keep talking) and the rendered transcript (transcript, needed to bring the screen back). Those two diverge — the transcript holds notices and errors that were never sent to the model — so saving only one would give you either a session you cannot continue or a blank screen you can.

Auto-save is always on: App::maybe_autosave runs after every loop iteration and writes when the conversation has settled and actually changed.

module doc and VERSION

L1–L19

VERSION is bumped only on an incompatible change, so an old build refuses a newer file instead of mis-parsing it. Note the discipline in Session below: the ledger field was added without a bump, because #[serde(default)] plus serde's ignore-unknown-fields behaviour makes that change compatible in both directions.

1//! Saving and loading conversations to disk.
2//!
3//! A session captures both the model conversation (`history`, needed to
4//! continue) and the rendered transcript (needed to restore the screen). Files
5//! are pretty-printed JSON, one per session, in a sessions directory.
6 
7use std::path::{Path, PathBuf};
8use std::time::{SystemTime, UNIX_EPOCH};
9 
10use anyhow::{Context, Result, bail};
11use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
12 
13use crate::app::Entry;
14use crate::ledger::Ledger;
15use crate::openrouter::Message;
16 
17/// The on-disk format version. Bumped only on an incompatible change so an old
18/// loader refuses a newer file rather than mis-parsing it.
19pub const VERSION: u32 = 1;

struct Session

L20–L36

The on-disk shape. history and transcript are the two halves described in the intro; prompt_history is your typed prompts for ↑ recall, which is why recall survives a /save → /load round-trip.

model is recorded but not applied on load — the running model is fixed at startup, so loading a session saved under a different one keeps the current model and posts a notice about the difference (see App::apply_session).

21#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
22pub struct Session {
23 pub version: u32,
24 /// Unix seconds when saved.
25 pub saved_at: u64,
26 /// The model in use when the session was saved.
27 pub model: String,
28 pub history: Vec<Message>,
29 pub transcript: Vec<Entry>,
30 pub prompt_history: Vec<String>,
31 /// Cumulative token spend. Added after `VERSION` 1 without a bump: it
32 /// defaults when absent, and older builds ignore the unknown field, so
33 /// files stay readable in both directions.
34 #[serde(default)]
35 pub ledger: Ledger,
36}

L37–L56

Stamps VERSION and the current time; everything else is moved in. Being a constructor rather than a struct literal at the call site means no caller can forget the version field or invent a timestamp.

39 pub fn new(
40 model: String,
41 history: Vec<Message>,

43 prompt_history: Vec<String>,
44 ledger: Ledger,
45 ) -> Self {

fn save

L57–L67

sanitize first, always — before any path is built. create_dir_all makes the sessions directory on demand, so a fresh checkout needs no setup step.

to_string_pretty rather than compact JSON: session files are meant to be readable and diffable when something goes wrong.

58/// Write `session` to `<dir>/<name>.json`, creating `dir` if needed.
59pub fn save(dir: &Path, name: &str, session: &Session) -> Result<PathBuf> {
60 let name = sanitize(name)?;
61 std::fs::create_dir_all(dir)
62 .with_context(|| format!("creating sessions directory {}", dir.display()))?;
63 let path = dir.join(format!("{name}.json"));
64 let json = serde_json::to_string_pretty(session).context("serialising session")?;
65 std::fs::write(&path, json).with_context(|| format!("writing {}", path.display()))?;
66 Ok(path)
67}

fn load

L68–L84

The version check happens after deserialising, which is the right order — a future format that still parses as this struct would otherwise be silently accepted with missing meaning.

A failed load leaves the current session completely untouched: App::load_named only replaces state on Ok, so a typo'd name costs you nothing.

68 
69/// Read `<dir>/<name>.json`.
70pub fn load(dir: &Path, name: &str) -> Result<Session> {
71 let name = sanitize(name)?;
72 let path = dir.join(format!("{name}.json"));
73 let text = std::fs::read_to_string(&path)
74 .with_context(|| format!("no session {name:?} at {}", path.display()))?;
75 let session: Session = serde_json::from_str(&text)
76 .with_context(|| format!("reading session {}", path.display()))?;
77 if session.version != VERSION {
78 bail!(
79 "session {name:?} has format version {} but this build reads version {VERSION}",
80 session.version
81 );
82 }
83 Ok(session)
84}

fn list

L85–L104

Names of saved sessions, sorted, for the /load picker.

An unreadable directory returns an empty Vec rather than an error (let Ok(entries) = ... else { return Vec::new() }), because "no sessions yet" and "no directory yet" should look the same to the user — and App::open_load_picker turns an empty list into a helpful notice.

85 
86/// Names (without extension) of saved sessions, sorted.
87pub fn list(dir: &Path) -> Vec<String> {
88 let Ok(entries) = std::fs::read_dir(dir) else {
89 return Vec::new();
90 };
91 let mut names: Vec<String> = entries
92 .flatten()
93 .filter_map(|e| {
94 let path = e.path();
95 if path.extension()?.to_str()? == "json" {
96 path.file_stem()?.to_str().map(str::to_string)
97 } else {
98 None
99 }
100 })
101 .collect();
102 names.sort();
103 names
104}

default_name and exists

L105–L117

default_name is session-<unix-seconds>. Every launch starts under one of these, which is what stops two concurrent runs from overwriting each other before you name anything.

exists is used in two places worth knowing: /fork refuses to overwrite an existing name, and reset_conversation only rewrites the file if there already was one — so /clear on a fresh session does not litter the directory.

105 
106/// A default, unique-ish name for `/save` with no argument.
107pub fn default_name() -> String {
108 format!("session-{}", now_secs())
109}
110 
111/// Whether a session file exists on disk.
112pub fn exists(dir: &Path, name: &str) -> bool {
113 match sanitize(name) {
114 Ok(name) => dir.join(format!("{name}.json")).is_file(),
115 Err(_) => false,
116 }
117}

fn rename

L118–L138

Refuses to clobber an existing target, but succeeds when nothing is saved under the old name yet — in that case the name simply becomes current and the next auto-save writes there.

That second behaviour is what makes /rename work immediately after launch, before the first turn has produced a file.

The old != new guard lets renaming a session to its own name be a no-op rather than an error.

118 
119/// Rename a session file `<old>.json` → `<new>.json`.
120///
121/// Refuses to clobber an existing `<new>` file. If nothing is saved under `old`
122/// yet, this succeeds without moving anything — the name simply becomes current
123/// and the next save writes there.
124pub fn rename(dir: &Path, old: &str, new: &str) -> Result<PathBuf> {
125 let old = sanitize(old)?;
126 let new = sanitize(new)?;
127 let new_path = dir.join(format!("{new}.json"));
128 if old != new && new_path.exists() {
129 bail!("a session named {new:?} already exists");
130 }
131 let old_path = dir.join(format!("{old}.json"));
132 if old_path.exists() {
133 std::fs::rename(&old_path, &new_path).with_context(|| {
134 format!("renaming {} to {}", old_path.display(), new_path.display())
135 })?;
136 }
137 Ok(new_path)
138}

fn sanitize — a small security boundary

L139–L152

A session name is user-typed and becomes a path, so this matters. It refuses separators and traversal rather than trying to normalise them.

Why refuse instead of sanitise: normalisation is where path bugs live — strip ../ and ....// becomes ../. Rejecting anything containing /, \, or .. is a rule with no clever cases, and it is called at the top of every function here that builds a path.
139 
140/// Reject a name that could escape the sessions directory. A session name is
141/// user-typed and becomes a path, so this is a small security boundary: refuse
142/// separators and parent traversal outright rather than trying to normalise.
143fn sanitize(name: &str) -> Result<&str> {
144 let name = name.trim();
145 if name.is_empty() {
146 bail!("session name must not be empty");
147 }
148 if name == "." || name == ".." || name.contains(['/', '\\']) || name.contains("..") {
149 bail!("invalid session name {name:?}: names cannot contain path separators or '..'");
150 }
151 Ok(name)
152}

fn now_secs

L153–L159

Unix seconds, with unwrap_or(0) for the pre-1970 clock case. A wrong timestamp is not worth failing a save over — the value is only used for display and for generating default names.

153 
154fn now_secs() -> u64 {
155 SystemTime::now()
156 .duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH)
157 .map(|d| d.as_secs())
158 .unwrap_or(0)
159}

What the tests cover

216 lines against a temporary directory. The round-trip test is the important one: save, mutate, load, and assert the conversation and the transcript come back identical.

sanitize gets its own battery — ../escape, a/b, ., .., empty and whitespace-only names. Version mismatch is checked to produce a refusal rather than a partial parse, and rename is checked to refuse clobbering an existing file while still succeeding when nothing is saved under the old name yet.

app.rs

1025 lines of code · 1823 lines of tests

All application state and every transition on it. The agentic loop's decisions live here; main.rs only supplies events and runs what this returns.

uses command, exec, files, input, ledger, openrouter, protocol, sandbox, session

used by main, ui, session

The biggest file, and the one to read most carefully. Almost every method here is a pure state transition: it mutates App and returns either nothing or a Vec<Message> meaning "send this next". No method in this file performs network I/O or spawns a process — that separation is what makes 1,800 lines of tests possible without any mocking.

The return-type convention is the agentic loop. When a method returns Some(messages), main.rs spawns a request with them; when it returns None, the turn has ended and control returns to you. Trace Option<Vec<Message>> through this file and you have traced the loop.

Two parallel records to keep straight, because their divergence explains a lot of the code:

  • history: Vec<Message> — what the model sees. Wrapped in protocol tags, and sometimes rolled back (see retry_after).
  • transcript: Vec<Entry> — what you see. Holds notices, errors, and raw frames that were never sent anywhere.

Both are saved to the session file, because you need the first to keep talking and the second to get your screen back.

enum Entry — the display transcript

L1–L51

One rendered block in the transcript. Kept separate from Message — as the doc comment says — so the UI can show things that are never sent to the model.

Notice how much richer this is than the conversation: Malformed keeps the raw text of a rejected reply so you can see exactly what the model said, Notice and Error are local-only, and Frame holds raw protocol payloads.

Why Frame is always recorded, not only in debug mode: it means turning /debug on reveals traffic that already happened rather than only what comes next. Debug is a pure view toggle, which is far more useful when something has just gone wrong.

CommandResult is Boxed because CommandOutput is much larger than the other variants and an enum is sized by its largest member.

FetchResult joins the result variants. It is boxed because FetchOutcome is a wide struct and an un-boxed variant would grow every Entry in the transcript to match it — the same reason CommandResult is boxed.

17/// One rendered block in the transcript. Kept separate from [`Message`] so the
18/// UI can show things (errors, notices) that are never sent to the model.
19#[derive(Debug, Clone, Serialize, Deserialize)]
20pub enum Entry {
21 User(String),
22 /// A model reply that parsed cleanly into a protocol action.
23 Action {
24 action: Action,
25 usage: Option<Usage>,
26 },
27 /// A reply that reached us but violated the protocol. `raw` is kept so the
28 /// user can see exactly what the model said.
29 Malformed {
30 reason: String,
31 raw: String,
32 },
33 /// The outcome of a command the user allowed.
34 CommandResult(Box<CommandOutput>),
35 /// The outcome of a file read. Unlike the others, no approval preceded it.
36 ReadResult(ReadOutcome),
37 /// The outcome of a URL fetch. Like a read, no approval preceded it.
38 FetchResult(Box<FetchOutcome>),
39 /// The outcome of a file write the user allowed.
40 WriteResult(WriteOutcome),
41 /// A command the user refused.
42 Denied(String),
43 /// A raw protocol payload crossing the boundary. Always recorded; shown only
44 /// in debug mode, so toggling `/debug` reveals earlier traffic too.
45 Frame {
46 direction: Direction,
47 body: String,
48 },
49 Error(String),
50 Notice(String),
51}

Direction and Choice

L52–L85

Two small enums with one method each. Direction::arrow gives the →/← the debug view prints; Choice::toggled is what ←/→/Tab call in the approval modal.

Choice is not Serialize — a modal is never in flight when a session is saved, since saving only happens at idle.

52 
53/// Which way a protocol frame travelled.
54#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Serialize, Deserialize)]
55pub enum Direction {
56 /// Harness → model.
57 Sent,
58 /// Model → harness.
59 Received,
60}
61 
62impl Direction {
63 pub fn arrow(self) -> &'static str {
64 match self {
65 Self::Sent => "→",
66 Self::Received => "←",
67 }
68 }
69}
70 
71/// Which button the approval modal has focused.
72#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
73pub enum Choice {
74 Allow,
75 Deny,
76}
77 
78impl Choice {
79 pub fn toggled(self) -> Self {
80 match self {
81 Self::Allow => Self::Deny,
82 Self::Deny => Self::Allow,
83 }
84 }
85}

struct Pending — an action awaiting your decision

L86–L98

The modal's state. edit_plan is the field that matters.

For an edit, the full rewrite was already computed during pre-flight and is stored here. On approval it becomes the write that actually runs — so the bytes that land are exactly the ones the diff showed you. The file is not re-read or re-matched after you click Allow, which would open a window for it to change underneath you.

None for every other action.

86 
87/// An action awaiting the user's decision. Holds the approvable action for
88/// display (shell, write, edit, or — under `--confirm-reads` / `--confirm-fetch`
89/// — read and fetch; never a terminal `Response`).
90#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
91pub struct Pending {
92 pub action: Action,
93 pub selected: Choice,
94 /// For an edit, the full rewrite prepared during pre-flight. On approval it
95 /// becomes the write that actually runs, so the diff the user saw is exactly
96 /// what lands. `None` for every other action.
97 pub edit_plan: Option<crate::files::EditPlan>,
98}

struct Picker

L99–L107

The /load overlay. Read the doc comment carefully: this is a UI overlay, not a conversation status — it coexists with Status::Idle.

That is why main.rs checks app.picker().is_some() separately from app.is_busy(): the picker owns the keyboard without the app being busy.

The session list is snapshotted when the picker opens, so the list cannot shift underneath a selection.

99 
100/// The `/load` session picker overlay. A UI overlay, not a conversation status:
101/// it coexists with `Status::Idle`.
102#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
103pub struct Picker {
104 /// Saved session names, snapshotted when the picker opened.
105 pub sessions: Vec<String>,
106 pub selected: usize,
107}

enum Status — the state machine

L108–L120

Five states, and this is the machine the whole program runs on:

Idle → Waiting (request sent) → Streaming (first token arrived) → either Idle (a Response ended the turn) or AwaitingApproval → Running → back to Waiting with the result.

is_busy() is simply "not Idle", and that single predicate gates all prompt editing.

108 
109#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
110pub enum Status {
111 Idle,
112 /// A request has been sent but no token has arrived yet.
113 Waiting,
114 /// Tokens are streaming in.
115 Streaming,
116 /// The approval modal is up for a proposed command.
117 AwaitingApproval(Pending),
118 /// An approved command is executing.
119 Running,
120}

struct App — the whole state

L121–L210

Thirty fields. Rather than reading top to bottom, group them:

  • Conversation — transcript, history, status, model.
  • View — scroll, follow, tick, debug, streaming.
  • Loop control — iterations/max_iterations, retries/max_retries/retry_anchor, generation.
  • Capabilities — sandbox, confirm_reads.
  • Money — ledger, price_in/_out, request_started.
  • Persistence — sessions_dir, current_session, last_saved, autosave_failed.

Three doc comments here explain decisions rather than fields, and are worth reading: sandbox is an Option field rather than a constructor argument to avoid threading a macOS-only type through ninety-odd test call sites; ledger survives /clear because the tokens were really bought; last_saved is a (history.len(), transcript.len()) fingerprint that works precisely because both only ever grow within a session.

Two new fields. confirm_fetches is the --confirm-fetch switch, kept separate from confirm_reads because the risks differ.

Why pending_fetch exists at all: a read is synchronous, so App just does it. A fetch is network I/O and needs a task, a generation tag and a cancel channel — all of which live in main.rs. Rather than let App spawn (and pull tokio into the one file with no I/O), the dispatch parks the URL here and the event loop collects it. It is a one-field outbox.
121 
122pub struct App {
123 pub input: Input,
124 pub transcript: Vec<Entry>,
125 /// Conversation as sent to the model. Diverges from `transcript`, which
126 /// also holds local-only entries.
127 pub history: Vec<Message>,
128 pub status: Status,
129 pub model: String,
130 /// Rows scrolled down from the top of the rendered transcript.
131 pub scroll: u16,
132 /// When true, the view sticks to the bottom as new content arrives.
133 pub follow: bool,
134 pub should_quit: bool,
135 /// Frame counter used to animate the waiting indicator.
136 pub tick: usize,
137 /// Model round-trips since the user last typed. Bounded so a model that
138 /// keeps proposing commands cannot loop forever.
139 pub iterations: usize,
140 pub max_iterations: usize,
141 /// When true, the transcript also shows raw protocol frames.
142 pub debug: bool,
143 /// Filesystem access for `<ai-harness-read>`. Set by `main` once the
144 /// sandbox exists; `None` only in tests that never read a file, which is
145 /// why this is a field rather than a constructor argument — the alternative
146 /// is threading a macOS-only `Sandbox` through ninety-odd test call sites.
147 pub sandbox: Option<Sandbox>,
148 /// When true, a read waits for approval like a command or a write. Off by
149 /// default: a read is non-mutating and confined to the working directory,
150 /// and making context-gathering silent is the point of having the element.
151 pub confirm_reads: bool,
152 /// When true, a fetch waits for approval. Separate from `confirm_reads`
153 /// because the risks differ: a read is confined to the working directory,
154 /// while a fetch is an outbound request to a host the model chose.
155 pub confirm_fetches: bool,
156 /// A fetch the dispatch approved but that `main` still has to spawn.
157 ///
158 /// Reads run inline because they are synchronous; a fetch is network I/O
159 /// and needs the same cancellation and generation machinery as a command,
160 /// which lives in the event loop rather than here.
161 pending_fetch: Option<String>,
162 /// Cumulative token spend for the session. Survives `/clear`: the tokens
163 /// were really bought, whether or not the conversation was kept.
164 pub ledger: Ledger,
165 /// Per-million-token prices, if the operator supplied them. Runtime config,
166 /// so deliberately not part of the persisted [`Ledger`].
167 pub price_in: Option<f64>,
168 pub price_out: Option<f64>,
169 /// When the in-flight request went out, for the ledger's waiting time.
170 request_started: Option<std::time::Instant>,
171 /// Consecutive malformed replies in the current streak; reset on success.
172 pub retries: usize,
173 pub max_retries: usize,
174 /// History length before the current streak of malformed replies, so a
175 /// give-up can roll the whole failed exchange back out of context.
176 retry_anchor: Option<usize>,
177 /// Highlighted entry in the completion menu. Clamped on read rather than on
178 /// write, since the list shrinks as the typed prefix narrows.
179 completion_cursor: usize,
180 /// The reply text accumulated so far while streaming. Display-only — the
181 /// authoritative text arrives with the final completion, so this is cleared
182 /// before the reply is committed.
183 pub streaming: Option<String>,
184 /// Identifies the current in-flight task. Bumped whenever a task is spawned,
185 /// and again on cancel, so updates from an abandoned task can be dropped.
186 generation: u64,
187 /// Prompts the user has submitted this session, oldest first, for Up/Down
188 /// recall. Kept separate from `history` (which is the model conversation)
189 /// and preserved across `/clear`.
190 prompt_history: Vec<String>,
191 /// While browsing `prompt_history`, the entry currently shown; `None` when
192 /// editing a fresh line.
193 history_index: Option<usize>,
194 /// The `/load` session picker, when open.
195 picker: Option<Picker>,
196 /// Directory where `/save` and `/load` read and write session files.
197 sessions_dir: PathBuf,
198 /// The session name auto-save writes to. Updated by save/load/rename/fork.
199 current_session: String,
200 /// Fingerprint of the last persisted state, so auto-save skips redundant
201 /// writes. `(history.len(), transcript.len())` — both only grow within a
202 /// session, so a change here means something was appended.
203 last_saved: (usize, usize),
204 /// Set when an auto-save write fails, so the error is reported once rather
205 /// than on every turn; cleared on the next successful save.
206 autosave_failed: bool,
207}
